course.title: Git and Version Control
course.description: Understand Git as snapshots, hashes and pointers rather than a list of commands, so that branching, merging, rebasing, undoing and sharing become predictable.
course.audience: A capable adult who has used a terminal a little and works with files that change, whether code, writing or data. Assumes the first two lessons of Linux and the Command Line and the hash digest idea from How Computers and Networks Work. No prior Git is needed.

paragraphs: Git is a program that keeps the history of a project, and its design is simple enough to describe completely. Each saved state, called a commit, is a snapshot of every file in the project at one moment, named by a hash computed from its contents and linked to the commit that came before it. A branch or a tag is a small pointer that holds the name of one commit, so making a new branch copies nothing, and moving one changes which commit it names.

Git is usually learned as a list of commands, which are easy to forget and easy to misuse when nothing explains what they do. With the picture of commits and pointers in mind, each command becomes a description of what happens to them. A merge of two diverged branches compares each tip with the commit where their histories split, a rebase copies commits onto a new parent and so gives them new hashes, and a reset moves the current branch to another commit. The result of each can be worked out before it is run.

That matters most when something goes wrong. Commits are never altered once they exist, so a commit that seems to be lost is usually still in the repository, whereas edits that were never committed have no such protection. The other danger is rewriting history that other people have already copied, because their copies then no longer match yours, and with the picture you can tell which commands do that before you run them.
outcomes: You'll be able to predict what git status shows after a sequence of edits.
You'll be able to explain a commit, a hash and a branch as objects and pointers.
You'll be able to tell a fast-forward from a three-way merge and resolve a conflict.
You'll be able to choose between merge and rebase and say when rewriting is unsafe.
You'll be able to pick the right undo and recover a commit with the reflog.
You'll be able to find the commit that introduced a bug in a handful of tests.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on How Computers Solve Problems, Linux and the Command Line, How Computers and Networks Work.

modules.title: Snapshots and history
modules.description: What a commit is, the three places a change lives, how Git names things, and how to read history.

modules.title: Branches, merging and undoing
modules.description: Branches as pointers, merging and conflicts, rebase, undoing safely, and finding the commit that broke something.

modules.title: Working with others
modules.description: Remotes, review workflows, and tags and messages that keep a project's history useful.

concepts.title: Repository
concepts.summary: The project's files together with the full history of every saved state.

concepts.title: Commit
concepts.summary: A saved snapshot of the whole project with a message, an author, a time and a link to the commit before it.

concepts.title: Distributed version control
concepts.summary: Every clone holds the complete history, so almost every operation works offline.

concepts.title: Working tree
concepts.summary: The files you edit on disk.

concepts.title: Index (staging area)
concepts.summary: The proposed next commit; git add copies a file's current content into it.

concepts.title: Tracked and untracked
concepts.summary: A file is tracked once it is in the index or the last commit; git commit -a includes changes to tracked files but never untracked ones.

concepts.title: Content addressing
concepts.summary: An object's name is a hash of its content, so identical content always has the same name and different content a different one.

concepts.title: Object types
concepts.summary: A blob holds file content, a tree lists names and the objects they point to, a commit points to one tree and its parents, and a tag names a commit.

concepts.title: Hash chain
concepts.summary: A commit's hash includes its parents' hashes, so changing an old commit changes it and every commit after it.

concepts.title: Revision name
concepts.summary: HEAD is the current commit, HEAD~n is its n-th ancestor along first parents, and a branch or tag names the commit it points at.

concepts.title: Range A..B
concepts.summary: The commits reachable from B but not from A.

concepts.title: Diff
concepts.summary: The line-by-line difference between two states: working tree and index, index and HEAD, or two commits.

concepts.title: Branch
concepts.summary: A movable name that points to one commit, stored as a 41-byte file holding the 40-character hash and a newline.

concepts.title: HEAD
concepts.summary: A pointer to the current branch, so a new commit advances that branch.

concepts.title: Detached HEAD
concepts.summary: HEAD points straight at a commit, so new commits belong to no branch and can be lost.

concepts.title: Fast-forward
concepts.summary: When the current branch's tip is an ancestor of the other branch, merge just moves the pointer forward and creates no commit.

concepts.title: Three-way merge
concepts.summary: When both branches have new commits, Git combines the changes of each since their merge base into a new commit.

concepts.title: Merge commit
concepts.summary: A commit with two parents.

concepts.title: Conflict
concepts.summary: Git cannot choose between changes that touch the same lines, or adjacent lines, since the merge base.

concepts.title: Conflict markers
concepts.summary: <<<<<<< HEAD begins your side, ======= separates, and >>>>>>> branch ends the other side.

concepts.title: Resolution
concepts.summary: Edit the file to the intended result, remove the markers, git add it and commit; git merge --abort returns to the state before.

concepts.title: Rebase
concepts.summary: Replaying a branch's commits one by one on top of a new base, which creates new commits.

concepts.title: Linear history
concepts.summary: A history with no merge commits, which rebase produces and merge does not.

concepts.title: Shared history rule
concepts.summary: Do not rewrite commits that others already have, because their copies will no longer match.

concepts.title: restore
concepts.summary: Discards edits in the working tree or unstages a file; it does not touch history.

concepts.title: reset modes
concepts.summary: git reset moves the branch to another commit; --soft leaves changes staged, --mixed leaves them unstaged and --hard discards them.

concepts.title: revert
concepts.summary: Makes a new commit that undoes an earlier one, so published history stays intact.

concepts.title: Reflog
concepts.summary: A local log of where HEAD has pointed, which can recover commits that no branch reaches.

concepts.title: Bisect
concepts.summary: A binary search through history: Git checks out the middle commit, you say good or bad, and the range halves.

concepts.title: Number of steps
concepts.summary: Searching n commits takes at most ceil(log2 n) tests, so 1,000 commits need 10.

concepts.title: Pickaxe
concepts.summary: git log -S 'text' lists commits that changed the number of occurrences of that text.

concepts.title: Remote and remote-tracking branch
concepts.summary: A remote is another copy of the repository, and origin/main is your record of where its main branch was when you last fetched.

concepts.title: Fetch and pull
concepts.summary: fetch downloads new commits and moves origin/main; pull is fetch followed by a merge or rebase into your branch.

concepts.title: Rejected push
concepts.summary: A push is refused if it would discard commits the remote has, which means you must integrate them first.

concepts.title: Pull request
concepts.summary: A hosting-service feature, not part of Git, that proposes merging a branch and holds the discussion and checks.

concepts.title: Trunk-based development
concepts.summary: Everyone merges small changes to one main branch at least daily, hiding unfinished work behind flags.

concepts.title: Long-lived branch
concepts.summary: A branch that lives for weeks or releases, which makes integration costly later.

concepts.title: Tag
concepts.summary: A fixed name for a commit; an annotated tag is an object with a message, a lightweight tag is a plain pointer.

concepts.title: Semantic version
concepts.summary: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: increase MAJOR for incompatible changes, MINOR for compatible features and PATCH for compatible fixes.

concepts.title: Commit message
concepts.summary: A short summary line, a blank line and a body saying why; conventional commits prefix the type, such as fix: or feat:.

concepts.title: Ignore file
concepts.summary: Patterns for untracked files Git should not list; it has no effect on files already tracked.

lessons.title: Why keep a history

reveal.text: The names order the files and nothing more. To learn what changed between `report_v2` and `report_v3` you must open both and compare them yourself.

lead.text: Copying a file before changing it works for a day or two. A name can say that two files are different, but it cannot say **what changed** between them, who changed it, or why.

Three needs follow from this, and version control exists to meet them. You need to **go back** to an earlier state when a change turns out to be a mistake. You need to **see what changed and why**, which means a description attached to every saved state. And you need to let several people work **in parallel** without overwriting one another.

afterFigure.text: A **version control system** is a tool that keeps this record for you, so that the saved states, their descriptions and their order live in one place instead of in file names.

diagram.alt: On one side a folder of five files named report.docx up to report_final_REAL.docx, with nothing saying how they differ. On the other side a row of five commits, each with a short message and an arrow back to the one before.
diagram.caption: Both hold five versions of the same report. Use the buttons to switch between the folder and the history.

lead.text: Git, the version control system this course is about, calls each saved state a **commit**. You create one deliberately, at a moment when the project is in a state worth keeping, and you give it a short message saying what the state adds or fixes. Git records the message together with your name, the time, and the project's files as they stand at that moment.

One item in the figure has not been described yet, and it is what turns separate commits into a history. Each commit also records its **parent**, the commit that was current when it was made, so that the commits form a chain running back in time. Reading the chain from the newest commit, you can walk back through every earlier state, and the first commit in a project is the only one with no parent.

afterFigure.text: A commit's description is part of the commit, and not a name attached to a file, so it cannot drift away from the state it describes.

diagram.alt: A commit drawn as a box with five fields: message, author, time, parent and snapshot. A second view shows three commits in a chain, each pointing to the one before, the first with no parent.
diagram.caption: A commit carries its own description and a link to its parent. Use the buttons to see one commit and then a chain.

reveal.text: Each commit points back to the one before it, so D leads to C, C to B and B to A. A, being first, has no parent at all.

lead.text: It is easy to picture a commit as a list of the lines you changed, because that is how changes are usually shown on screen. A commit is better pictured as a complete photograph of the project: a project of ten files has ten files in every commit, including the nine you did not touch. Git does not copy those nine again, since it can see they are identical to the ones in the previous commit, but as far as you are concerned the commit holds all ten.

The commits, together with the project's current files, are what is called a **repository**. In a folder on your computer a repository looks like the ordinary project files plus one hidden folder named `.git`, which is where the history lives.

afterFigure.text: The differences between two commits are worked out when you ask for them, by comparing the two snapshots. Later lessons show how to ask.

reveal.text: The new commit holds a snapshot of all 200 files. Git reuses the 197 unchanged files from the previous commit instead of copying them again, which is why the picture and the storage differ.
A commit has to exist before it can be recovered. The morning's edits were never committed, so they were only ever on the failed disk.

lead.text: Early version control tools kept the history on one central server. When you **clone** a repository, you download the entire history, every commit back to the first one, and you can read it, compare any two commits, and make new commits with no network connection at all. A system built this way is called **distributed**, because the full history is spread across every machine that has a clone.

In the figure Alice makes a new commit on her laptop, pushes it to a hosting service, and Ben fetches it from there to his own laptop. Only these last steps need a network, and the repositories themselves are equals.

afterFigure.text: This is also why a repository is a partial safeguard. If the hosting service disappeared, any clone could restore it, but only commits that someone had actually shared would be in those clones, so version control is **not a backup** of work you have not committed.

diagram.alt: Three boxes in a row: Alice's laptop, a hosting service and Ben's laptop. Each holds a row of commits. In the first view only Alice has the fourth commit, in the second the hosting service has it too, in the third all three have it.
diagram.caption: Every box holds the whole history, not just the newest files. Use the buttons to follow one new commit around.

lead.text: Linus Torvalds began writing Git in April 2005, after the Linux kernel project lost its free access to the BitKeeper tool it had been using.

GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket are separate companies' websites that host repositories so that people can share them. They are built on Git, but they are not Git, and a repository on your own disk is a full repository without any of them.

reveal.text: Sending a commit is the one step that needs the other machine. The clone holds the whole history, so reading it, comparing commits and committing all carry on while the service is down.

lessons.orientation: Say what problems version control solves and what a commit, a repository and a clone are.
lessons.nextAction: Look at the three places a change lives before it is committed, and predict what git status shows.

blocks.text: A **version control system** keeps a project's history as a series of saved states, each stored with a message that says what it adds, and because every state also records the one that came before it, the states form a chain that can be followed from the newest to the oldest.

A record of that kind lets you return to the state before a mistake and see exactly what separates any two states. Git is the version control system that most software teams use, and the saved state it records is called a **commit**.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what a commit, a repository and a clone are, and why Git and GitHub are different things.
intro.whyItMatters: Version control is the shared habit behind almost all software work, and the rest of Git is easier once its basic unit is clear.

recap.keyIdea: A commit is a saved snapshot of the whole project with a message and a link to its parent, and a repository holds every commit, so every clone carries the full history.

blocks.text: You saw that a folder of copies records which files exist but not what changed, and that a commit adds a message, an author, a time and a parent to a snapshot of the whole project. Because every clone downloads the complete history, almost everything you do in Git, apart from pushing and fetching, works with no network.

Git is the program that keeps this history on your own disk, and GitHub and GitLab are services that host copies of it. Version control also keeps only the states you commit, so it does not replace a backup of work you have not yet saved to the history.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at the three places a change lives before it becomes a commit.

lessons.title: Working tree, index and repository

lead.text: When you open a project folder and edit a file, you are changing the **working tree**, the files as they sit on your disk. Git keeps two other versions of the project out of sight: the **last commit**, the most recent snapshot in the history, and the **index**, a draft of the *next* commit that you build up by hand, also called the staging area.

The command `git add` copies a file's content, as it is at that moment, from the working tree into the index, and `git commit` then turns the index into a new commit. In the figure, `a.txt` starts at version 1 in all three places, and each button shows one more step of an edit, an add, a second edit and a commit.

afterFigure.text: Look at the third view. Adding recorded version 2, and the later edit made version 3, which the index has never seen. The working tree can therefore disagree with the index, and the index with the last commit, both at once.

reveal.text: The second `git add` copied the newest edit into the index, so the working tree and the index agree and only the staged difference from the last commit remains.

lead.text: The command `git status --short` prints one line per file that differs somewhere, and each line starts with two characters followed by the file name. The **left** character compares the index with the last commit, so it describes what is *already staged*. The **right** character compares the working tree with the index, so it describes what is *not yet staged*. A blank means the two places agree.

That is why an edited file that has not been added shows as a blank followed by M, and why the same file after `git add` shows an M followed by a blank. A file that has been added and then edited again differs in both pairs and shows MM. Switch views to see the codes for files that are new or deleted.

afterFigure.text: A file Git has never been told about is **untracked**, and it shows as two question marks. A **tracked** file is one that is in the last commit or in the index.

steps.headline: Follow a.txt through edit, add, edit and commit, and count how many different versions Git is holding.

workedSteps.text: `a.txt` starts at version 1 in all three places, and `git status` prints nothing.
An edit changes only the working tree. The right-hand column turns to M.
`git add` copies the working tree's content into the index. Now the working tree and the index agree, so the left-hand column shows M.
A second edit changes only the working tree again, so both columns show M.
Compare the version that each of the three places holds.

lead.text: It is fair to ask why Git has an index at all, when it could commit the working tree directly. You may have fixed a typo in three files and begun a larger change in two others, and a single commit holding all five files would carry a message that fits neither piece.

With an index you add only the three files of the fix and leave the other two for a later commit. Even inside one file you can split the work with **git add -p**, which shows each changed hunk, a block of neighbouring changed lines, and asks whether to stage it.

reveal.text: The commit holds `b.txt` exactly as it was in the last commit, because that is what the index held. Your edit stays in the working tree, and the next `git status` lists it as modified and unstaged.

lead.text: Because there are three places, there are two comparisons to look at. The command **git diff** compares the working tree with the index, so it shows the edits you have not yet added. The command **git diff --cached** compares the index with the last commit, so it shows exactly what a commit made now would contain.
The option **-a** on `git commit` stages every change to a *tracked* file for you before committing, but `commit -a` never adds new files, so a forgotten new file is simply left out of the commit.

reveal.text: Plain `git diff` would show only the edits you have not staged. Adding `--cached`, or its synonym `--staged`, switches the comparison to the index against the last commit.
Only `a.txt` goes into the commit. The new file stays untracked, and `git status` afterwards still shows `?? new.txt`.

lessons.orientation: Predict what git status shows after a sequence of edits, adds and commits.
lessons.nextAction: Look inside the repository at how Git stores a commit, and see what a hash is.

blocks.text: After you edit a file in a Git project, `git status` lists it as modified but *not staged for commit*, and after `git add` the same file is listed under *changes to be committed*, although the file on disk is exactly the same in both reports. The difference is where Git is holding the change: in the files on disk, called the **working tree**, in a draft of the next commit called the **index**, or in a commit that has already been made.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read the two columns of git status --short and say what git add and git commit will do to each file.
intro.whyItMatters: Almost every Git surprise comes from not knowing which of the three places holds a change.

recap.keyIdea: A change moves from the working tree to the index with `git add`, and from the index to a commit with `git commit`, and `git status` compares the three places in pairs.

blocks.text: Git keeps three versions of your project at once: the working tree you edit, the index that holds the draft of the next commit, and the last commit. The left column of `git status --short` compares the index with the last commit, and the right column compares the working tree with the index.

Because `git add` records a file's content at the moment you run it, a later edit needs adding again, and the index is what lets you commit part of your work. The option `-a` stages tracked files only, so a new file has to be added by name.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson opens up the repository to see what a commit actually is and why it has a hash for a name.

lessons.title: Objects and hashes

lead.text: The file in the figure holds the text `hello` and a newline. Run it through the hashing function SHA-1 and out comes `ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a`, forty characters long. A **hash** of this kind is computed from the content alone, so the same content always gives the same hash, and changing even one letter gives a result that looks unrelated.

SHA-1 produces 160 bits, and a hexadecimal character carries 4 bits, so the hash is 160 ÷ 4 = 40 characters. Git uses these hashes as names, and every object it stores is filed under the hash of its content.

reveal.text: Dividing the bits by the bits per character gives the length. The same sum turns SHA-1's 160 bits into the 40 characters of every full Git hash, and 7 of those are usually enough to point at one.

lead.text: A **blob** holds the contents of one file, and nothing else: not its name, and not where it lives. Git computes its hash over a short header, the word `blob`, a space, the size in bytes and a zero byte, followed by the content. For `hello` and a newline that is `blob 6`, a zero byte, and the six bytes, and hashing them gives the `ce01362` start you saw.

A **tree** is a folder. It lists, for each entry, a mode, a name and the hash of what it holds, which is a blob for a file and another tree for a sub-folder. A **commit** points to one tree, the root of the whole project at that moment, together with the hashes of its parents, the author, the time and the message. The figure shows the three kinds linked: the commit leads to the project and, through the parent link, to the commit before it.

afterFigure.text: Because a commit points to a whole tree, the commit really is a snapshot of every file, as the first lesson said. It is not a list of differences.

lead.text: Because an object is named by its content, two files with the same text produce one blob however many folders contain them, and a file that did not change between two commits produces no new blob at all: the new commit's tree simply lists the old blob's hash again. This is what makes the whole-snapshot picture affordable. Committing a project of a thousand files after one edit adds one new blob, the trees on the path from that file up to the root, and one commit.

reveal.text: A blob has no name inside it, and a commit points to exactly one of these. Folders are what it represents.
same is stored once and other once, so two blobs serve three files.
The commit's hash is computed from its content, and that content includes the hash of its parent.

lead.text: A commit object contains the hash of its parent, and a commit's own hash is computed over everything it contains. Edit the message of commit 3 and its hash changes, because its content changed. Commit 4 contains the hash of commit 3, so commit 4 now contains different content, and its hash changes too, and so does commit 5's, all the way to the tip. Commits 1 and 2 come before the edit, contain nothing that changed, and keep their hashes.

This chain is what makes history tamper-evident: nobody can alter an old commit without also changing the name of every later one. It is also the reason a rewrite of history is visible to anyone who already has the old commits.

afterFigure.text: Git still uses SHA-1 by default. A collision, two different files with one SHA-1, was demonstrated in 2017, and Git has had experimental support for SHA-256 repositories, with 64-character hashes, since version 2.29 in October 2020.

lessons.orientation: Explain how Git names content with a hash, what the three object types are, and why changing history changes every later hash.
lessons.nextAction: Learn to name commits in ways shorter than a hash, and to read the history with log, diff and ranges.

blocks.text: Run `git log` in any repository and every commit appears under a name made of hexadecimal characters. The name is computed from the commit's content, so the same content gives the same name on every computer, and a name made in this way is called a **hash**.
Because the name follows the content, changing a single letter in a file gives it a completely different name, while two objects with the same name have the same content.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what a hash is, name the three object types, count objects, and say which commits change when one is edited.
intro.whyItMatters: Hashes explain why Git can detect changes and why rewriting history is visible to others.

recap.keyIdea: Git names every blob, tree and commit by the hash of its content, and because a commit contains its parent's hash, changing one commit changes all those after it.

blocks.text: A hash is a fixed-length fingerprint of content: SHA-1 gives 160 bits, which is 40 hexadecimal characters. Git stores file contents as blobs, folders as trees, and each commit as a pointer to one tree plus its parents, author and message, and identical content is stored once because identical content has one name.

A commit contains the hash of its parent, so editing a commit changes its hash and the hash of every commit that comes after it, while the commits before it are unchanged. That is why rewriting shared history shows up for everyone who already has the old commits.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson uses short names for commits, and reads history with log, diff and ranges.

lessons.title: Reading history

lead.text: The simplest way to read a project's past is `git log`, which prints each commit with its hash, author, date and message, newest first. Adding **--oneline** shortens each entry to an abbreviated hash and the first line of the message, and adding **--graph --all** draws every branch, not only the one you are on, with lines showing which commit descends from which.

In the first view of the figure two commits, c1 and c2, are shared, and after c2 the history split in two: main went on with c3, and a branch named feature received f1. Names such as main and feature are labels attached to commits, and HEAD marks the commit you are looking at now.

afterFigure.text: By default `git log`, run on one branch, lists only the commits reachable from it.

diagram.alt: A commit graph with c1 and c2 in a line, then c3 on main and f1 on feature, both pointing back to c2. The views highlight different ranges: main..feature selects f1, feature..main selects c3, and plain main selects c1, c2 and c3.

reveal.text: The notation counts parent links, one per tilde step, so HEAD~2 is two steps back along the chain.

lead.text: Commands that take a commit accept several kinds of name. A full hash works, and so does any abbreviation of it that is long enough to be unique, commonly seven characters. A branch name stands for the commit it points to. And **HEAD** stands for the commit you currently have checked out, so that **HEAD~1** is its parent, **HEAD~2** is its parent's parent, and in general `HEAD~n` is n steps back.

The tilde counts *parent links* and has nothing to do with dates: two commits made on the same afternoon can be five steps apart, and a commit made last year can be one step back if nothing came between them.

afterFigure.text: Because every commit records its parent, these names need no table or numbering.

reveal.text: HEAD~3 is three steps back from the newest commit, so subtract the step count from the newest commit's number.

lead.text: It is often useful to ask what one branch has that another lacks. The notation **main..feature** answers it: it selects every commit that can be reached from `feature` by following parent links, *except* those that can also be reached from `main`. In the history drawn at the start of the lesson, `feature` reaches f1, c2 and c1, and `main` reaches c3, c2 and c1, so the only commit that `feature` reaches alone is f1, and `main..feature` is a range of one commit.

Reversing the names reverses the question. `feature..main` selects the commits that `main` has and `feature` lacks, which here is c3. The two ranges happen to hold one commit each in this history, but they are different commits, and in general they hold different numbers. The command `git log main..feature` lists a range, and `git rev-list --count main..feature` prints how many commits it holds.
Read A..B aloud as what B has that A does not, and the order stops being a trap.

reveal.text: feature..main means the commits main can reach that feature cannot.

lead.text: Once you can name a commit you can look inside it. **git show** followed by a name prints the commit's message and the change it made, shown as a **diff**: lines starting with a minus sign were removed, lines with a plus sign were added, and the grey lines around them are context.

The same format answers the comparisons from the last lesson. Plain **git diff** compares the working tree with the index, **git diff --cached** compares the index with the last commit, and **git diff A B** compares two commits. To ask who last changed each line of a file, **git blame** prints the file with the commit and author that most recently touched every line.

afterFigure.text: Blame answers *which commit*, and the commit's message then says why.

reveal.text: The answer is a short word that is also what you do with someone when you are looking for the source of a mistake.
`git log` lists everything reachable from where you are, including the commits that came before the branch was made.

lessons.orientation: Use log, show, diff, blame and revision names such as HEAD~2 and A..B to answer questions about a project's past.
lessons.nextAction: Learn what a branch really is: a pointer to one of these commits.

blocks.text: Run `git log` and Git prints the commits of a project from the newest to the oldest, which it does by starting at the commit you are on and following each commit's record of its parent.
With the chain to follow, you can find the commit that last changed a line, see exactly what it changed and read the message that says why it was made.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to resolve a name like HEAD~2, count the commits in a range, and choose the command that shows a change or its author.
intro.whyItMatters: These are the commands you use every day to understand code you did not write.

recap.keyIdea: A revision name picks a commit by following parent links, A..B selects what B has and A lacks, and show, diff and blame read what changed and who changed it.

blocks.text: Every commit knows its parent, so `HEAD~2` means two parent links back and not two days ago, and `A..B` selects the commits reachable from `B` but not from `A`, so reversing the names asks the opposite question. `git log` with `--graph --all` draws the whole shape of the history.
Once a commit has a name, `git show` prints what it changed, `git diff` compares any two states, and `git blame` says which commit last changed each line, whose message then explains why.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson shows that a branch is only a name attached to one of these commits.

lessons.title: Branches are pointers

lead.text: Run `cat .git/refs/heads/main` inside a repository and the file holds forty characters, the hash of one commit, plus a newline, so it is 41 bytes. A **branch** is a name for a commit, nothing more. Creating a branch copies no files and makes no commit, which is why branches are so cheap.

Another file, `.git/HEAD`, records where you are. Normally it holds the line `ref: refs/heads/main`, which says that **HEAD** is attached to the branch `main`. The figure begins there and then runs four commands, so watch which label moves each time.

afterFigure.text: Two things can move: a branch label, which is a pointer to a commit, and HEAD, which is a pointer to a branch. Every Git command that changes where you are moves one of them or the other.

diagram.alt: A commit graph with three commits and labels for branches. Five views show main at c3 with HEAD on main, then a new branch x created at the same commit, then HEAD moved to x, then a commit made on x, and finally a commit made on main after switching back, which splits the history.
diagram.caption: Branch labels are pointers to commits, and HEAD points to the branch you are on. Use the buttons to follow five commands.

reveal.text: A branch is a label on a commit, and a commit can carry several labels.

lead.text: Switching branches, with **git switch x**, changes the contents of `.git/HEAD` and updates your working tree to match the commit that `x` names. No branch label moves. When you then make a commit, Git creates the new commit with the current commit as its parent and moves *the branch that HEAD is attached to* to the new commit. Other branches stay exactly where they were.

That explains the last two views in the figure of branch labels, on the screen before last. After the commit on x, x points at c4 while main still points at c3. Switching back to main and committing again starts a second line of history from c3, and now the two branches have diverged. The history is the same graph of commits as before, and the branches are just two names on it.
The word *current branch* therefore means the branch HEAD is attached to, and the commit you are on is the one that branch points to.

reveal.text: A commit moves the branch that HEAD is attached to, and a branch is a file holding a hash. `.git/HEAD` keeps naming the branch, and the file for the other branch stays as it was.

steps.headline: Trace the pointers through a short session, starting with main at c3 and HEAD on main.

workedSteps.text: `git branch x` adds the label x to c3. HEAD stays on main.
workedSteps.math: main: c3, x: c3, HEAD on main

workedSteps.text: `git switch x` moves HEAD onto x.
workedSteps.math: main: c3, x: c3, HEAD on x

workedSteps.text: A commit c4 is made. HEAD is on x, so x moves to c4 and main stays.
workedSteps.math: main: c3, x: c4, HEAD on x

workedSteps.text: `git switch main` moves HEAD back onto `main`, and then a new commit c5 is made.

reveal.text: Commits are only kept alive by something that reaches them. While you made these two, only HEAD pointed at them, and switching to main moved HEAD away.

lead.text: If you run `git checkout` followed by a commit hash, or a tag, HEAD stops pointing at a branch and points straight at that commit. Git calls this a **detached HEAD** and warns you. You can look around and even commit, and each commit moves HEAD along, but no branch label comes with it. When you then switch to a branch, HEAD leaves the new commits behind, and nothing named reaches them.

The commits d1 and d2 in the figure are made in the detached state, and after the switch they are drawn in red because no branch can reach them. The fix is to give them a name *before* leaving, with **git switch -c rescue**, since a new branch always starts at the commit you are on.

afterFigure.text: A detached HEAD is therefore not an error. It is a state in which the only record of where you are is HEAD itself.

diagram.alt: A commit graph in which HEAD points directly at commit c2 rather than at a branch. In later views two commits d1 and d2 are made from there, then HEAD returns to main and no branch reaches them, and finally a branch called rescue is shown keeping them.
diagram.caption: A detached HEAD points at a commit instead of a branch. Use the buttons to follow what happens to commits made in that state.

A ref file holds the hash and one newline, so the size is the length of the hash plus one.

lessons.orientation: Explain what a branch and HEAD are, and say which pointer moves on commit, branch and switch.
lessons.nextAction: Combine two branches with a merge, and tell a fast-forward from a three-way merge.

blocks.text: Open `.git/refs/heads/main` in a repository and you find a single line, the hash of one commit. A **branch** is therefore a name for one commit, and creating one is as cheap as writing that line.
Git keeps one more marker, HEAD, that says which branch you are on, and a commit moves the branch HEAD is on and no other.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say which label moves on commit, branch and switch, and recognise a detached HEAD.
intro.whyItMatters: Everything in the next six lessons, from merging to undoing, is movement of these pointers.

recap.keyIdea: A branch is a small file naming one commit, HEAD names the branch you are on, and a commit moves only the branch HEAD is attached to.

blocks.text: You saw that creating a branch makes no commit, that switching moves only HEAD, and that a commit advances the current branch and leaves the others behind. A branch is forty characters and a newline, so it costs almost nothing.
When HEAD points at a commit instead of a branch it is detached, and commits made there are reached by no name once you leave, unless you create a branch first with `git switch -c`.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson brings two diverged branches back together with a merge.

lessons.title: Merging

reveal.text: When one branch's history already contains the other's, Git has nothing to combine, so it only moves a label.

lead.text: Suppose you branched `feature` off `main` at c2, made one commit f1 on it, and want that work on `main`. If `main` has made no commits since, `main`'s tip c2 is an *ancestor* of `feature`'s tip f1, which means the history of `main` is already contained in `feature`'s. Git then has nothing to combine: it slides `main`'s label forward to f1. This is called a **fast-forward**, and it creates no commit.

The situation is different if main has also moved on, as in the third view, where main gained c3 while feature gained f1. The two tips are now on different lines of history and neither contains the other, so Git records the result as a commit of its own.

afterFigure.text: The one question that decides between the two is whether the target branch's tip is an ancestor of the branch being merged.

diagram.alt: Two commit graphs. In the first pair of views main has not moved since feature branched, so merging slides main's label forward to f1. In the second pair both branches have new commits, c3 and f1, and merging creates a new commit M with two parents.

lead.text: When both branches have moved, Git looks for the most recent commit that both can reach, called the **merge base**. In the figure the merge base of `main` and `feature` is c2. It then compares each tip with that base: c3 against c2 gives `main`'s changes, and f1 against c2 gives `feature`'s. Because it uses three snapshots, the base and the two tips, this is called a **three-way merge**.

The file view shows why the base matters. In the first case ours edited line one and theirs edited line three. Against the base, each line was changed by exactly one side, so Git keeps each change and the result has both. If it compared only the two tips, a line that differs would look the same whichever side had changed it, and Git could not tell which version to keep.

afterFigure.text: For each line the rule is short: if only one side changed it, take that side. If both sides changed it differently, Git cannot decide, which is a conflict.

reveal.text: The merge base is the latest commit that both branches can reach.
A line that differs between the two tips could have been changed by either side. Only a third snapshot, the base, shows which side left it as it was.

steps.headline: main holds c1 to c4 and feature holds c1, c2, f1 and f2. Merge feature into main and count what main reaches.

workedSteps.text: Find the merge base. Both branches reach c1 and c2, and c2 is the latest of them.
Main has moved on, so main's tip c4 is not an ancestor of f2, and a fast-forward is impossible. Git does a three-way merge.
It applies c3 and c4's changes and f1 and f2's changes to the base and records a new commit with two parents, c4 and f2.
Main now reaches everything that either branch reached, along with the merge commit itself.

lead.text: The commit that a three-way merge makes is special in one way: it has **two parents**, the old tip of the branch you were on and the tip of the branch you merged in. Its snapshot is the combined result. After `git merge feature` on `main`, `git log --graph` shows the two lines of work running side by side and joining at that commit, and every commit from both branches is reachable from `main`.

A merge does not delete anything on the branch you merged in, which still points where it did. **git merge --no-ff** makes a merge commit even when a fast-forward was possible, and **git merge --ff-only** refuses to create a merge commit.

afterFigure.text: The choice between these is a choice about the *shape* of the history, and neither one changes the files you end up with.

reveal.text: The option forces a merge commit even where a fast-forward was possible.
Each side changed different lines, so Git keeps all three changes: two from main and one from feature.

lessons.orientation: Predict whether a merge is a fast-forward or creates a merge commit, and what the result contains.
lessons.nextAction: Meet the case Git cannot merge by itself: two edits to the same lines, and how to resolve it.

blocks.text: Take a repository in which `main` and `feature` both grew from the commit c2. Combining the two lines of history is called a **merge**, and Git can usually do it without being told which changes to keep, because it compares each tip with the commit where the lines split, c2, and takes a change from whichever side made it.
A merge can take one of two forms, and which one depends on a single fact about the graph, whether either tip already contains the other.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say whether a merge is a fast-forward, and count the commits after a three-way merge.
intro.whyItMatters: Merging is how every collaboration on a Git project eventually comes together.

recap.keyIdea: A merge is a fast-forward when the target's tip is an ancestor of the other tip, and otherwise a three-way merge from the merge base that ends in a commit with two parents.

blocks.text: If the branch you are on has made no commits of its own, Git moves its label forward and creates nothing. If both branches have moved, Git compares each tip with their merge base, applies both sets of changes, and records a merge commit that has two parents.

The merge copies nothing over and deletes nothing, so every commit from both branches is reachable afterwards. The options `--no-ff` and `--ff-only` choose the shape of the history, and do not change the files.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson covers what happens when both sides changed the same lines.

lessons.title: Merge conflicts

reveal.text: Two unchanged lines separate the edits, so neither one overlaps the other and the merge combines them without a conflict.

lead.text: A merge compares each branch with the commit where they split, so two edits can be combined whenever neither disturbs the other.

A **merge conflict** arises when Git cannot tell what the combined text should be. The clearest case is the one in the last view: both sides changed line 2, one to `main` and the other to `other`, and a line cannot hold both.

afterFigure.text: A conflict is not an error and nobody has made a mistake.

lead.text: It is tempting to think that edits on different lines can never conflict, and the first two cases support that, but the third does not. When ours edits line 2 and theirs edits line 3, Git reports a conflict even though no line was edited twice. The reason is that Git does not merge line by line. It works on **hunks**, a changed line together with the position it sits in, and two changes that touch or abut each other count as one place where the two histories disagree.

A single unchanged line between the edits, as in the second case, is enough to separate them. In practice this means that two people working in the same few lines of a file will meet conflicts, and two people in different parts of the file almost never will.

reveal.text: Neighbouring edits become one place of disagreement, not two.

lead.text: When a merge conflicts, Git leaves the file in your working tree with both versions in it, separated by markers. The line `<<<<<<< HEAD` begins the section holding your side, the version on the branch you were on. A line of seven equals signs divides the two. The line `>>>>>>> other` ends the section, and the name after it is the branch being merged, whose text sits just above it. The status of the file is shown by `git status --short` as `UU`, which means unmerged on both sides.

To resolve the conflict you edit the file so that it holds the text you actually want, and delete all three marker lines. You might keep one side, keep the other, or write something combining both, as the figure shows. Then you run `git add` on the file to say it is resolved, and `git commit` to finish the merge. If you would rather start over, `git merge --abort` returns the project to how it was before the merge.

afterFigure.text: Resolving does not mean choosing a whole side. It means deciding what the file should say, and the markers are only a help to see the two candidates.

Two further views show the same place after resolving, by combining both texts or by taking one.

steps.headline: Resolve a conflict in f from start to finish.

workedSteps.text: `git merge other` stops with a conflict, and `git status --short` shows `f` as `UU`.
Open f, where the two versions sit between markers, and rewrite the region as the text you want.
The three marker lines belong to neither version, so they come out of the file as well.
`git add f` and then `git commit` complete the merge as a merge commit with two parents.

lead.text: Resolving a conflict becomes a long job when a branch has lived for weeks, because the other branch has moved a long way. Two habits keep conflicts small: keep branches short, and merge the main branch into your own branch regularly, so that you meet each disagreement while it is still small.
A merge tool, a program that shows the base and both sides together, can make a large conflict easier to read, but everything a tool does can also be done by editing the file.

reveal.text: A file stops being unmerged once you have added it, so only the file you have not added is still listed as UU.

lessons.orientation: Read conflict markers, say which side each part belongs to, and predict whether two edits will conflict.
lessons.nextAction: Replay your commits on top of another branch with rebase, and see what it does to their hashes.

blocks.text: In a configuration file, one line reads `timeout = 10`. One branch changes it to `timeout = 30` and another changes it to `timeout = 60`. A line cannot hold both, and Git has no way of knowing which value is right, so when the branches are merged it stops and writes both versions into the file between marker lines, leaving the decision to you. This is a **merge conflict**.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to predict whether two edits conflict, read the markers, and finish a conflicted merge.
intro.whyItMatters: Every team meets conflicts, and a clear way of reading them is what keeps them minor.

recap.keyIdea: Git merges edits that do not touch, treats edits on the same or neighbouring lines as a conflict, and leaves both versions between markers for you to turn into the text you want.

blocks.text: Edits that are separated by at least one unchanged line merge silently, and edits on the same or neighbouring lines produce a conflict because Git merges in hunks. In a conflicted file the section after `<<<<<<< HEAD` is your side, the section before `>>>>>>>` and the branch name is the incoming side, and a line of equals signs divides them.

To resolve, edit the file to the text you want, delete the marker lines, add the file and commit, or abandon the attempt with `git merge --abort`. Short branches and regular merges from `main` keep each conflict small.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson shows another way of combining branches, rebase, and what it does to commit hashes.

lessons.title: Rebase and rewriting history

lead.text: A merge joins two lines of history. **Rebase** does something different: it changes where your branch *starts*. In the first view, `feat` branched from base, and `main` has since moved on by two commits. Running `git rebase main` while on `feat` finds the commits that `feat` has and `main` lacks, f1, f2 and f3, and sets them aside. It then moves `feat` to `main`'s tip, m2, and replays the three commits one after another on top of it.
Every commit of `feat` is a *copy* made on the new starting point, which is why the figure names them with primes, and the three originals are left behind with nothing pointing to them.

afterFigure.text: If a replayed commit changes lines that `main` also changed, Git stops with a conflict exactly as in a merge, and you resolve it, add the file and run `git rebase --continue`.

diagram.alt: Three graphs of the same project. The first has main two commits ahead of the point where feat branched, and feat holding three commits. The second shows feat rebased: copies of the three commits sit after main's tip and the originals are greyed out. The third shows a merge instead, with a new commit joining the two lines.
diagram.caption: Use the buttons to compare the history before, after a rebase, and after a merge. Primed names are new commits.

reveal.text: A commit's hash covers its parent's hash, and the parent of the first replayed commit has changed.

lead.text: The copies are not identical to the originals. Each has the same author, the same message and the same change, but a commit records its parent, and the parent of f1' is m2 where the parent of f1 was base. A different parent means different content for the commit object, and so a different hash, as in the lesson on objects. The change then runs down the branch: f2' has f1' as its parent and so also a new hash, and f3' likewise. All three commits are new objects.

This answers a common worry that rebase *moves* commits and loses something. It copies them, and the originals stay in the repository until Git's garbage collection removes objects that nothing reaches, which normally happens weeks later.

reveal.text: The range is what feat has that main lacks, and the commits of feat are now on top of main.

steps.headline: Branch feat has two commits and main has moved four commits past the common base. Count the commits in the log of feat after rebasing it onto main.

workedSteps.text: Before the rebase, feat's log is the shared base commit and its own two commits.
The rebase replays f1 and f2 on main's tip, so the log runs through main's four commits first.
The log of feat now starts at the last replayed commit and runs back to the shared base.

lead.text: The third view of the figure on the replaying screen shows the same project merged, so the history says honestly that two things were done in parallel and brought together. Rebase gives a history that reads as one thing done after the other, which is easier to follow and to bisect, at the price of recording a story that did not quite happen in that order.
Both produce the same files, and in one respect rebase carries a risk that merge does not.

Running **git rebase -i HEAD~3** opens an editor listing your last three commits, oldest first, each preceded by the word `pick`. You change the word to choose what happens: **pick** keeps the commit as it is, **reword** keeps it but lets you rewrite the message, and **squash** folds a commit into the one above it, combining their changes into one commit. You can also reorder the lines or delete one to drop that commit.

With a typo fix and a second typo fix squashed into the commit above, three commits become one, which is a good way to tidy a series of small corrections before sharing it. As with any rebase, every commit from the first edited line onwards is a new commit with a new hash.

reveal.text: Three commits become one, and the other four are untouched.

lead.text: Rebase and interactive rebase create new commits and move a branch label to them. On a branch that only you have, that is harmless, since nobody else refers to the old commits. If you have already pushed the branch and a teammate has pulled f1, the situation is different. Their repository has f1, and yours now has f1' instead, so the two histories have diverged from the point of the rewrite, and Git will refuse a normal push of your version.

To push the rewritten branch you would have to force it, replacing what is on the server, and that is what makes rebase dangerous for *shared* history: your teammate's commits are no longer part of the branch, and they must untangle the difference. The working rule is therefore plain. Rewrite your own unpublished commits as freely as you like, and do not rewrite commits that others have already taken.

afterFigure.text: A lighter form of force, `git push --force-with-lease`, refuses to overwrite commits you have not seen.

reveal.text: The three untouched commits keep their hashes and are still in your branch. The two reworded commits are copies with new hashes, so your teammate's versions of them are no longer part of it.
`squash` folds a commit into the one above it. `pick` keeps a commit as it is, `reword` keeps it and changes only its message, and removing the line drops it.

lessons.nextAction: Choose the right undo for a mistake, and recover a lost commit with the reflog.

blocks.text: A **rebase** takes the commits that are on your branch and not on another, and replays them one after another on top of the other branch's tip, so that your branch appears to have started there.

That gives a history that reads as one thing done after another, and the same replaying lets you reorder, combine and reword commits before you share them. Whether it is safe to do so depends on who else already has the commits being replayed.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what a rebase does to hashes and ranges, compare it with a merge, and say when it is safe.
intro.whyItMatters: Rebase is where Git's hash chain stops being theory and starts to matter for teamwork.

recap.keyIdea: Rebase replays commits on a new starting point, which gives each a new hash, and it is safe only for commits that nobody else has.

blocks.text: A rebase finds your branch's commits, sets them aside, moves the branch to the new base and replays them, so the history becomes a straight line. Each replayed commit has a new parent and therefore a new hash, so afterwards the range main..feat holds the same number of commits as before but they are new objects.

Merge records what happened and rebase tidies the story, and both give the same files. Interactive rebase can squash, reword and reorder, and because every rewrite replaces commits, it should be confined to commits that nobody else has taken.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at undoing mistakes, from a bad edit to a rewritten history.

lessons.title: Undoing things

reveal.text: `git restore` is named for what you want done to the file: put it back as it was.

lead.text: There is no single undo command in Git, because a mistake can sit in four different places and each needs a different tool. An edit you have made in a file and not staged is undone by **git restore** followed by the file name, and a change you have staged is undone by **git restore --staged**, which takes it out of the index and leaves your edit in the file.

Once the change is in a commit, the question becomes whether anyone else has the commit. If it is only on your machine, **git reset** can move the branch back so that the commit is no longer on it. If it has been pushed and others may have pulled it, rewriting is unsafe, and **git revert** is used instead, which adds a new commit that reverses the old one.

afterFigure.text: The further a mistake has travelled towards shared history, the more careful the undo must be.

diagram.alt: Four rows of mistake, undo command and result. An edit in the working tree is undone with git restore. A staged change is unstaged with git restore --staged. A local commit is undone with git reset. A pushed commit is undone with git revert, which adds a new commit.

lead.text: The edits in your working tree are not in any commit and not in the index, so Git has no copy of them. When `git restore` overwrites a file, the previous contents are gone, and the same is true of any command that discards uncommitted work, including the `--hard` mode of `reset`.
That makes it worth running `git diff` before `git restore`, to look at exactly what is about to be lost.

reveal.text: reset moves the branch label back along the parent links, the same way as HEAD~2 counts them.

lead.text: Every `git reset` starts the same way: it moves the current branch's label back to the commit you name, and the commits after it are no longer on the branch. What differs is how far the change reaches. With **--soft** nothing else changes, so the files from the removed commit stay in the index, exactly as if you had just staged them and not yet committed. With **--mixed**, which is the default, the index is reset too, so those files remain in the working tree but unstaged. With **--hard** the working tree is also reset, and the files from the removed commit disappear.

The figure uses a history of two commits, `one` and `two`, with `two.txt` added in the second, and runs `git reset HEAD~1`. In all three cases one commit remains. The difference is what happened to `two.txt`: staged under `--soft`, left only in the working tree under `--mixed`, and gone under `--hard`.

afterFigure.text: Reach for `--soft` to redo a commit with a different message or a different set of files, and use `--hard` only when you are sure you want the changes gone.

diagram.alt: Three boxes for the branch, the index and the working tree, shown for each mode of git reset. All three modes move the branch back one commit. Soft leaves the index and working tree alone. Mixed also resets the index. Hard resets the index and the working tree too.
diagram.caption: Each mode moves one step further. Orange boxes are the ones that changed. Use the buttons to compare soft, mixed and hard.

reveal.text: Git has no earlier version of the file to compare with, and the file is not in the index.

steps.headline: Recover a commit that a reset --hard seems to have destroyed, starting from commits one and two.

workedSteps.text: `git reset --hard HEAD~1` moves the branch back, so the branch now holds only `one`, and `two.txt` disappears from the working tree.
The commit `two` still exists as an object. `git reflog` lists where HEAD has been, and shows the commit as `HEAD@{1}`.
The branch has to move forward to `two` again, using the position the reflog showed.

lead.text: Reset removes commits from a branch, which is fine for commits only you have and harmful for commits others have pulled. **git revert** takes the opposite approach. Given a commit, it works out the change that commit made and applies the *reverse* of that change as a brand-new commit on top of the branch.

Nothing is deleted or rewritten, so a teammate who already has commit two can simply pull the revert on top of it. A revert does not erase the original from the record. It says, in the history itself, that the change was made and later undone, and that is often exactly what a team wants.

reveal.text: Revert adds a commit and removes none.

lead.text: Git keeps a private diary of your repository, the **reflog**. Each time HEAD or a branch moves, because of a commit, a reset, a switch or a rebase, Git adds a line with the commit's hash and a position such as `HEAD@{1}`, meaning where HEAD was one move ago. It is stored locally in your repository and is never pushed.

A commit that no branch reaches is not deleted at once. It stays as an object, and the reflog keeps a way to name it, for a default of about 30 days for unreachable entries and 90 for the rest. Until then `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}` or `git switch -c rescue` followed by the hash will get it back. The one thing that the reflog cannot restore is an edit that was never committed, since it was never an object.

reveal.text: `HEAD@{1}` is where HEAD was before the most recent move.

lessons.orientation: Choose the right undo for a mistake in the working tree, the index or the history, and recover a lost commit with the reflog.
lessons.nextAction: Find which commit introduced a bug using binary search.

blocks.text: Run `git reset --hard HEAD~1` and the newest commit seems to have vanished, since it no longer appears in `git log` and its files are gone from the working tree. The commit still exists, though, as an object in the repository, and Git keeps a record of where HEAD has been, the **reflog**, from which the commit can be brought back. An edit that was never committed has no such record, so a command that discards it destroys it for good.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to pick the right undo for a mistake, predict what each reset mode leaves behind, and recover a commit with the reflog.
intro.whyItMatters: Knowing which undo is safe is what lets you experiment with Git without fear.

recap.keyIdea: The right undo depends on where the mistake lives: restore for files and the index, reset for commits only you have, revert for shared commits, and the reflog to find a commit a reset has left behind.

blocks.text: `git restore` handles edits in the working tree and the index, and discards uncommitted work for good. `git reset` moves the branch back, and its modes decide whether the index and the working tree follow: soft changes neither, mixed resets the index, and hard resets both. `git revert` adds a new commit that reverses an old one and so is the safe choice for shared history.
A commit that a reset has moved off the branch is still recorded in the reflog, typically as `HEAD@{1}`, so committed work is rarely lost, while edits that were never committed cannot be recovered.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson uses the history to find which commit broke something.

lessons.title: Finding what broke

lead.text: You know that a commit at one end is good and a commit at the other is bad, so the first bad commit lies somewhere between. If you test the commit in the *middle*, its result tells you which half to keep.

That is binary search, as in the lesson on halving the problem in CS Basics, applied to history. With the bug first appearing at commit 637, ten tests in total are enough to narrow the window to a single commit.

afterFigure.text: Git automates the whole procedure with `git bisect`, which checks out the middle commit for you and asks only whether it is good or bad.

diagram.alt: A long bar standing for 1,000 commits with an orange window marking the commits that could still contain the first bad one. In five views the window shrinks from the whole bar to 500, 250, 125 commits and finally to a single commit after ten tests.
diagram.caption: Each test removes half of the remaining commits. Use the buttons to follow a search for a bug in a history of 1,000 commits.

reveal.text: Each test halves the number of commits that remain.

lead.text: Each test halves the window, so after k tests a window of n commits has shrunk to n ÷ 2^k, and the search ends when one commit remains. The most tests it can need is therefore the smallest k with 2^k at least n. For 1,000 commits, 2^9 is 512, which is too few, and 2^10 is 1,024, which is enough, so ten tests are the most it needs. For a million commits, 2^20 is 1,048,576, so twenty tests are enough.

The table shows how slowly the count grows. Every time the history doubles, bisect needs one more test, so a thousand times more commits costs only ten more. A test per commit grows a thousandfold, and this grows by ten, which is why the method stays practical on very large projects.

diagram.caption: The number of tests grows by one each time the history doubles.

steps.headline: Find the first bad commit among eight commits c1 to c8, where c1 is the first to follow a good commit and the bug arrived at c6.

workedSteps.text: The first bad commit is somewhere among all eight. Test the one in the middle, c4.
c4 is good, so the bug arrived later, and c5 to c8 remain.
Test the middle of what is left, c6. It is bad, so the first bad commit is c5 or c6.
workedSteps.math: c6 is bad, window: c5, c6

workedSteps.text: Two commits remain, and the search carries on until one is left.

lead.text: Start with `git bisect start`, then name the commit that is known to be bad, usually with `git bisect bad`, and one that was good, with `git bisect good` followed by its name. Git checks out the commit in the middle, you test it and say `git bisect good` or `git bisect bad`, and when the window is one commit Git reports it as the first bad commit.

The testing can be automated with **git bisect run** followed by a script or command. Git runs it at each step and reads its exit code: **0 means good**, and a code from 1 to 127, except 125, means bad. The code 125 means this commit cannot be tested, and Git skips it. The test must give the same answer each time it is run on a commit, because a test that fails at random will send the search into the wrong half and the result cannot be trusted.

afterFigure.text: Bisect needs no understanding of the code. It needs only a yes-or-no test.

lead.text: Bisect needs a test. Sometimes you have something else: a line of code that you know matters, and the question is when it appeared. For that, **git log -S** followed by a string, called the **pickaxe**, lists the commits in which the number of occurrences of the string changed, which means the commits that added or removed it.

The three tools answer different questions. Bisect answers *which commit made the test fail*, and needs a test. The pickaxe answers *when did this text appear or vanish*, and needs a string. Blame answers *who last changed this line*, and needs a file.

reveal.text: The code 125 means this commit cannot be tested, so bisect skips it and tests another. A code of 0 marks a commit good, and any other code from 1 to 127 marks it bad.
One wrong answer decides which half is kept, and c6 lay in the half that was discarded. The search ends on a commit at or before c4, which is the wrong one.
Each doubling of the history adds one test. Six thousand is four times fifteen hundred, which is two doublings, so bisect needs two more tests.

lessons.orientation: Use bisect and the pickaxe to locate the commit that introduced a bug, and compute how many steps bisect needs.
lessons.nextAction: Share history with other people: remotes, fetch, pull and push.

blocks.text: A test that passed on one commit fails on a later one, and between the two lie 1,000 commits, one of which introduced the failure. Testing every commit would take a long time, but the commit in the middle of the range can be tested at once, and whichever way its result falls it rules out half of the commits that remain.
Repeating that step is a binary search through the history, and Git automates it as **git bisect**.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute how many tests bisect needs, run a bisect, and choose between bisect and the pickaxe.
intro.whyItMatters: Finding the commit that broke something is the payoff of keeping a clean history.

recap.keyIdea: Bisect halves the range of suspect commits with each test, so it needs at most the smallest k with 2^k reaching the number of commits, and the pickaxe finds when a string was added or removed.

blocks.text: You know a good commit and a bad one, so testing the middle commit tells you which half holds the first bad commit, and each test halves the window. A thousand commits need at most ten tests and a million need at most twenty, since the count rises by one each time the history doubles.

`git bisect run` automates the tests with an exit code of 0 for good and 1 to 127, apart from 125, for bad, and the test must be deterministic. When you have a string and not a test, `git log -S` lists the commits that added or removed it.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson shares history with other people through remotes.

lessons.title: Remotes and sharing

reveal.text: Alice's repository has had no contact with the host since the push.

lead.text: A **remote** is a named link to another copy of the repository, reached over HTTPS or SSH. When you clone a repository, Git records the address you cloned from under the name **origin**, and it also creates a label, **origin/main**, which marks where the host's `main` was when you last talked to it. Such a label is called a **remote-tracking branch**.

The first view shows the state right after cloning, with every copy holding c0. In the second Bob pushes two commits, and then in the third Alice makes one of her own. Look at Alice's repository in the third view: her origin/main still says c0, although the host has moved on to b2.

afterFigure.text: The host's repository and yours are separate, and neither one learns about the other's new commits until a command moves them across.

diagram.alt: Three boxes for Alice's repository, the hosting service and Bob's repository, each with its commits and branch labels. After the clone every repository holds c0. Bob pushes two commits b1 and b2 to the host. Alice commits a1 locally, and her origin/main label still points at c0. After Alice fetches, origin/main moves to b2 while her main stays at a1.

lead.text: Three commands move commits between repositories. **git fetch** asks the host for commits you do not have, stores them, and moves `origin/main` to match. It changes nothing you are working on: your branch and your files stay as they are, so a fetch is always safe. **git pull** is a fetch followed by an integration, a merge by default, of `origin/main` into your current branch, and so it *does* change your branch and your working tree. **git push** does the reverse of a fetch: it uploads your commits and asks the host to move its `main` to your tip.

That distinction explains why origin/main is not live. It shows the host as it was at the last fetch, pull or push, and a fetch is the only way to refresh it without altering your own work. After a fetch, `git status` compares your branch with origin/main and reports how far ahead or behind, or diverged, you are.

steps.headline: Alice has one new local commit, a1, and Bob has pushed two, b1 and b2, from the same starting commit c0.

workedSteps.text: Alice runs `git push`. The host has commits she lacks, so it refuses her upload with the message rejected, fetch first.
`git fetch` brings b1 and b2 into her repository and moves origin/main to b2. Her main is still at a1.
`git status` now says the branches have diverged, with one commit on her side and two on the other.
`git pull --no-rebase` merges `origin/main` into `main`.

lead.text: The host will move its `main` only to a commit that contains its current `main` in its history, so that nothing already there is dropped. When Alice's a1 and Bob's b1 and b2 grew from the same c0, neither contains the other, and the host refuses with the words *fetch first*. The message is not about permission or a broken connection: it says that you have not yet seen everything the host has.

The fix has three steps. Fetch, so that you have the host's commits. Integrate them into your branch, either by merging origin/main or by rebasing your commits onto it. Then push again. After the merge in the last view of the figure on the previous screen, Alice's main contains b2, so the host accepts it as a plain advance.
Which integration to use is the same choice as before: merge keeps the real order of events, and rebase makes a straight line.

reveal.text: Ahead means the commits on her main that origin/main does not have.
A rebase makes a copy of each of her commits and adds no merge commit.

lead.text: There is one case where a push *should* replace what is on the host, which is after you have rewritten your own branch, for instance with a rebase. The host sees a branch whose history no longer contains its old tip, and refuses. The option `--force` overrides that refusal and replaces the branch regardless, so any commit that a teammate had pushed since your last fetch is silently dropped from the branch.

The safer form is **git push --force-with-lease**. It makes the push conditional: the host is asked to replace the branch only if it still points where *your* `origin/main` says it does. If someone has pushed in the meantime, the push fails and you fetch first.

reveal.text: It is the operation from the lessons on branches that joins two lines of history.
A fetch stores the host's commits and moves `origin/main`, but your branch is untouched, so it still lacks them. Merging or rebasing is what makes your branch contain them.

lessons.orientation: Explain fetch, pull and push, remote-tracking branches, and why a push is rejected.
lessons.nextAction: See how teams organise this sharing with pull requests and branching workflows.

blocks.text: When `git push` to a **remote** is refused with the words `rejected` and `fetch first`, nothing is wrong with the commit being pushed and nothing is wrong with the host. The host holds commits that your repository has never seen, and it will move its branch only to a commit that contains its current tip, so a push from a history that has diverged cannot be accepted as it stands. The message makes sense once you can see where each commit is and what your repository believes about the host.

Three commands, fetch, pull and push, carry commits between your repository and the host's, and they differ in whether they change your own branch. Knowing which one does lets you share work without being surprised by a rejected push or by a merge you did not intend, and it is the basis for deciding how to join your commits to the host's.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read how far a branch is ahead of or behind its remote, and fix a rejected push without forcing.
intro.whyItMatters: Sharing work is where most Git confusion starts, and it clears quickly once the bookmark idea is clear.

recap.keyIdea: origin/main is a bookmark that moves only when you fetch, pull or push, and a push is rejected when the host has commits you lack, which you fix by integrating them and pushing again.

blocks.text: A clone gives you the full history, your own main, and origin/main, which marks the host's main as of your last contact. Fetch updates that bookmark without touching your work, pull is a fetch followed by a merge, and push uploads your commits only if the host can simply move forward.

When the histories have diverged the host rejects the push with `fetch first`. You fetch, merge or rebase the host's commits into your branch, and push again, and you keep force pushes, preferably `--force-with-lease`, for branches you have rewritten that nobody else uses.

lessons.title: Collaboration workflows

reveal.text: Review comments and automatic checks live on the hosting service's page for the branch, and not in Git itself.

lead.text: Work on a shared project follows a pattern: you make a branch for one piece of work, push it to the host, and then ask for it to be merged into `main`. That request is a **pull request**. The feature is not a part of Git at all: it is offered by hosting services such as GitHub and GitLab (GitLab calls it a merge request), which add a page to each one where the change can be discussed.

On that page reviewers read the diff, leave comments on individual lines, and see the results of automatic checks such as a test run. Only branching, pushing and the final merge are Git operations, and the middle stages are the review process around them.

lead.text: Size is the main thing a team controls about a pull request. A reviewer can hold a hundred lines in mind and judge whether they are right, but with a thousand lines the reading becomes skimming, and mistakes pass through. A small change can also be reverted on its own, where a large one takes all its good parts with it.
A good pull request does one thing, has a short description of what and why, and has passing checks.
