reveal.text: Only pull request 4's change is reversed. The other nine stay in `main`, which is the advantage of keeping pull requests small.

lead.text: **GitHub flow** is the pattern described earlier in this lesson: branch from `main`, push, open a pull request, review, merge, and deploy. Main is always in a state that could go live, and each branch lives until its pull request is merged. It suits a team that ships one hosted version of a product again and again.

**Trunk-based development** pushes the same idea further. Developers merge small changes to one main branch, called the trunk, at least daily, and any branch lives for a day or two at most. That raises a question: how can half-finished work be merged without breaking the product? The usual answer is a **feature flag**, a switch in the code that keeps new behaviour hidden until it is ready, so that the code can be merged long before the feature is turned on.

afterFigure.text: The point of both is to keep branches short, because the cost of a branch is not in creating it, which is instant, but in how long it stays apart from main.

lead.text: Not every product has a single live version. A library may have users on version 2.x who need security fixes while version 3.x is under active development, and for such a case a team keeps a long-lived **release branch** for each supported version, and applies fixes to each of them separately.

A well-known description of this approach is Vincent Driessen's 'A successful Git branching model', published in January 2010. He later added a note to the article saying that it suits software that is released in explicit versions, and is a poor fit for web applications that are delivered continuously.

It is a switch in the code, and the word names the kind of marker it is.

lead.text: A team that depends on review can ask the hosting service to enforce it. A **protected branch** refuses direct pushes, and accepts a merge only when the rules are met, for example that the tests pass and that at least one other person has approved.

The rules are a team's decision and not a Git feature, but they make the earlier advice enforceable, and checks are what let a reviewer concentrate on design and leave the mechanical errors to the machine.

lessons.orientation: Compare trunk-based development, GitHub flow and long-lived release branches, and say what a pull request is for.
lessons.nextAction: Mark releases with tags and version numbers, and write messages that others can use.

blocks.text: Git places no limit on how a team uses it. It will let anyone with access push straight to `main`, leave a branch unmerged for six months, or merge a change of a thousand lines that no one else has read. A team that wants to avoid those outcomes has to agree a **workflow** on top of Git, a shared habit about how long branches live, how changes are reviewed and what a release looks like.

What matters in a workflow is how long a branch stays apart from main, because the longer it does, the more there is to review, the more is likely to conflict and the harder a mistake is to take back.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what a pull request is for, and choose a workflow for a described team.
intro.whyItMatters: Branches cost almost nothing in Git, and the workflow decides what they cost a team.

recap.keyIdea: A pull request is a hosting service's way of reviewing a branch before it is merged, and workflows differ mainly in how long branches live.

blocks.text: A pull request carries a branch through review and automatic checks before it is merged, and it is a feature of hosting services, not of Git. Small, focused pull requests are faster to review, cause fewer conflicts and can be reverted alone.

GitHub flow keeps a deployable main and short-lived branches, trunk-based development merges daily and hides unfinished work behind feature flags, and release branches serve products that must support several versions at once. Protected branches make the review and check rules binding.

lessons.title: Tags, versions and messages

reveal.text: A commit moves the branch that HEAD is on, as the lesson on branches showed, and a tag is not a branch, so it stays where it was put.

lead.text: A branch label moves forward with every commit made on it, which is useless for saying *this exact commit is version 1.0*. A **tag** is the answer: a name attached to one commit that never moves. Create it on the commit you release, with `git tag v1.0`, and it will name that commit for ever.

Git has two kinds of tag. A **lightweight tag** is only a pointer, like a branch that never moves, and `git cat-file -t` on it reports `commit`, because the name points straight at a commit. An **annotated tag**, made with `git tag -a v1.0 -m` followed by a message, is a real object of its own that records who tagged it, when, and with what message, and `git cat-file -t` reports `tag`.

afterFigure.text: Tags are only local until pushed. `git push` does not send them by default, and `git push origin v1.0` sends one.

diagram.alt: A line of commits with a branch label main and a tag label v1.0. In the first view both labels are on the same commit. After two more commits main has moved to the newest commit and v1.0 stays on the old one.

lead.text: Once releases have names, the names should carry meaning. **Semantic Versioning**, described at semver.org, gives each of the three numbers a job. The **patch** number goes up for a backwards-compatible bug fix. The **minor** number goes up for new functionality that is backwards compatible, and the patch number then goes back to zero. The **major** number goes up for a change that breaks existing users, and the minor and patch numbers then both go back to zero.
The point of the scheme is that a user reading only the number can tell what an upgrade risks: a patch should be safe to take, a minor should add without breaking, and a major needs care.

afterFigure.text: The left-hand number always outranks the right, and a bump resets everything to its right.

diagram.alt: A version number split into MAJOR, MINOR and PATCH boxes. The starting version is 2.4.1. A bug fix gives 2.4.2, a compatible feature gives 2.5.0, and a breaking change gives 3.0.0, with the changed boxes highlighted.
diagram.caption: A change of the left-hand number outranks one on the right, and it resets what lies to its right to zero. Use the buttons to apply each kind of change.

steps.headline: Start from 1.7.4 and apply a fix, a compatible feature and a breaking change, in that order.

workedSteps.text: A backwards-compatible fix raises the patch number.
A compatible feature raises the minor number and resets the patch number to zero.
A breaking change is made next.

reveal.text: A lightweight tag points straight at a commit, so `git cat-file -t` shows the commit's type. An annotated tag is an object in its own right and prints `tag`.

lead.text: The diff already records *what* changed, line by line, so the useful part of a commit message is the *why*: what problem the change solves, and why this approach. The conventional layout is a short summary line, a blank line, and then a body for the reason.

Some teams also write the summary in a machine-readable form. The **Conventional Commits** format begins each message with a type such as `feat` or `fix`, an optional scope in brackets, a colon and the summary, and marks a breaking change with an exclamation mark or a `BREAKING CHANGE` footer. Because a `feat` means a minor bump, a `fix` a patch bump and a breaking change a major bump, tools can read the messages since the last tag and choose the next version number themselves.

diagram.alt: A commit message laid out as a summary line, a blank line and a body. The first view shows a plain message whose body gives the reason. The second view shows a Conventional Commits message with a type, a scope and a breaking-change footer.
diagram.caption: A reader sees the summary first and the body only if they look further. Use the buttons to compare a plain message with a Conventional Commits message.

reveal.text: The diff already shows which lines changed. What does it not show?

lead.text: Some files do not belong in a repository: logs, build output, local settings, and above all secrets such as passwords and keys. A file named **.gitignore** lists patterns, such as `*.log`, for files that Git should treat as invisible. A new file matching a pattern never shows up as untracked, and `git add` will not stage it unless you force it.

The ignore rule has a limit that surprises people. It affects only *untracked* files. A file that is already tracked stays tracked after you add its name to `.gitignore`, and later edits to it still appear in `git status`. The same persistence applies to secrets. If a password was committed and pushed, deleting it in the next commit leaves it in every earlier commit and in every clone, so it cannot be taken back. The safe response is to treat it as exposed and change it, which is called rotating the secret, and cleaning the history is a second, optional step.

reveal.text: An ignored file does not appear in the untracked list.
The old password remains in the earlier commit and in every clone, so the secret has to be replaced. Replacing an exposed secret is called rotating it.

lessons.orientation: Name releases with tags and semantic versions, write commit messages others can use, and keep secrets and generated files out.
lessons.nextAction: You can now read and predict Git: status, history, branches, merges, rewrites, undo, remotes and releases. Apply that to your own repository.

blocks.text: A release of a program is one particular commit, and a project that has shipped version 2.4.1 has to be able to say which commit that is. Git provides a name for this purpose, the **tag**, and semantic versioning adds a convention for what the numbers inside such a name should mean, so that a version number tells a user what an upgrade is likely to change.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what a tag is, bump a version correctly, write a message that gives a reason, and respond to a leaked secret.
intro.whyItMatters: A history is only useful later if its releases are named and its messages say why.

recap.keyIdea: A tag names one commit for ever, semantic versioning gives its numbers a meaning, messages should say why, and a pushed secret has to be treated as exposed.

blocks.text: A tag is a name that does not move, annotated tags are objects of their own, and a version number written as MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH says whether a release is a fix, a compatible feature or a breaking change, with the numbers to the right reset to zero when one on the left goes up.

A good commit message gives a summary and the reason, and Conventional Commits makes the type readable by tools. A .gitignore hides untracked files and does nothing for tracked ones, and a password that has been pushed stays in the history, so it must be changed.

questions.prompt: How many of the five file names tell you what changed between one version and the next?
hints: Read the names: do they contain any description of a change?
A name such as `report_final` identifies a file, and nothing in it describes a difference.
Count the names that describe a change between versions.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The names only order the files. None of them says what changed, so the answer is 0.

questions.onCorrect: A name identifies a file but cannot hold a description of a change, which is what a commit message is for.

misconceptions.feedback: A name such as _v2 says only that the file is a second copy, and it does not describe any change.
All five have names, but a name labels a file and does not describe what changed.

questions.prompt: A folder holds `report.docx`, `report_v2.docx`, `report_v3.docx`, `report_final.docx` and `report_final_REAL.docx`. What do the file names tell you about how the versions differ?
hints: Read the names as a stranger would, and ask what you could infer about `report_v3` from its name alone.
A name can put files in an order. Ask whether it can also describe a difference between two of them.

acceptedIdeas: The names suggest an order, but say nothing about what changed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The names suggest an order, but say nothing about what changed

questions.onCorrect: A name identifies a file but cannot hold a description of a change, which is what a commit message is for.

misconceptions.feedback: A name such as `report_v2` says only that the file is a later copy. Nothing in it describes a change.
Nothing in a name such as `report_v3` records an author or a time.
Names such as v2, v3 and final do hint at an order, so calling them arbitrary goes further than the names justify.

choices.label: The names suggest an order, but say nothing about what changed
The names list the changes made in each version
The names record who made each version and when
The names are arbitrary, so they give no sign of which version came last

questions.prompt: Commits A, B, C and D were made in that order, and each one records its parent. Which commit is D's parent?
hints: The parent is the commit that was current when this one was made.

acceptedIdeas: Only C, the commit made just before D
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only C, the commit made just before D

questions.onCorrect: Each commit records only its parent, and the whole history is found by following those links back one at a time.

misconceptions.feedback: A is the oldest ancestor of D, but D does not point to it directly.
A, B and C are all ancestors of D, but a commit records one parent, not every earlier commit.
The newest commit has a parent like any other. Only the very first commit has none.

choices.label: Only C, the commit made just before D
Only A, the first commit in the project
A, B and C, every commit made before D
None, because D is the newest commit

questions.prompt: A project has ten files. You change one line in one of them and commit. How many files does the new commit's snapshot contain?
hints: Think of a commit as a photograph of the project.
A photograph shows everything in the project, not just what moved.
Count the files in the project, not the files you changed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A commit records the whole project, so the snapshot contains all 10 files, nine of them reused unchanged.

questions.onCorrect: Git reuses the nine unchanged files from the previous commit, so storing the full snapshot costs very little extra space.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the file you changed. A commit is a snapshot of the whole project, so unchanged files are in it too.
The nine unchanged files are in the snapshot, and so is the file you changed.

questions.prompt: A project has ten files. You change one line in one of them and commit. What does the new commit's snapshot contain?
hints: Think of a commit as a photograph of the project.
A photograph shows everything in the project, not just what moved.

acceptedIdeas: All ten files, as they are after the change
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: All ten files, as they are after the change

questions.onCorrect: Git reuses the nine unchanged files from the previous commit, so storing the full snapshot costs very little extra space.

misconceptions.feedback: A commit is a snapshot of the whole project, so it holds every file and not just the lines that changed.
The nine unchanged files are in the snapshot too, and so is the file you changed.
Git does reuse the nine unchanged files from the earlier commit when it stores the new one, but as far as you are concerned the new commit holds all ten and you can ask for any of them.

choices.label: Only the one file that changed
Only the one line that changed
All ten files, as they are after the change
The one changed line, with the other nine files left in the earlier commit

questions.prompt: You edit three files this morning without committing, and at noon the laptop's disk fails. You pushed your last commit to the hosting service yesterday. What can you get back from the hosting service?
hints: Ask what a commit is: something you create on purpose.
Edits that were never committed were never in the history.

acceptedIdeas: The commits you pushed yesterday, but not the morning's edits
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The commits you pushed yesterday, but not the morning's edits

questions.onCorrect: A repository keeps the states you commit and share. Work that exists only in an uncommitted edit has no copy anywhere else.

misconceptions.feedback: Git records a state only when you commit, and it does not watch the files between commits.
The commits you pushed were copied to the hosting service, so that history survives there.
A hosting service holds only what was pushed to it, and uncommitted edits are never pushed.

choices.label: Nothing at all, because the whole history was on the failed disk
The morning's edits, if the hosting service is still online
The commits you pushed yesterday, but not the morning's edits
The morning's edits, because Git tracks the files continuously

questions.prompt: Ben cloned a project of 3,000 commits and the hosting service is now offline. How many of the commits can he read?
hints: Ask what a clone downloads.
A clone downloads the whole history, not only the newest files.
Reading history needs no network once the clone exists.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A clone holds the complete history, so all 3,000 commits are on Ben's own disk.

questions.onCorrect: Reading history, comparing commits and committing locally all work offline, since only pushing and fetching need the other machine.

misconceptions.feedback: A clone does not download only the latest commit; it downloads every commit.
The service being offline stops pushing and fetching, but Ben's clone is already complete.

questions.prompt: Ben cloned a project of 3,000 commits, and the hosting service is now offline for a day. What can he do with his clone?
hints: Ask what a clone downloads.
A clone downloads the whole history, not only the newest files.
Reading and committing happen on your own machine, and only pushing and fetching need the other one.

acceptedIdeas: Read all 3,000 commits, compare any two of them and make new commits
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Read all 3,000 commits, compare any two of them and make new commits

questions.onCorrect: Reading history, comparing commits and committing locally all work offline, since only pushing and fetching need the other machine.

misconceptions.feedback: A clone downloads every commit back to the first one, so the older commits are on Ben's own disk as well.
The history was copied to Ben's machine when he cloned, so reading it needs no connection to the service.
Making a commit writes only to the local repository, and the service is needed just to push or fetch.

choices.label: Read all 3,000 commits, compare any two of them and make new commits
Read the history, but make no new commits until the service is back
Read only the newest commit, because the older ones stay on the service
Read nothing until the service is back, because the history is kept there

questions.prompt: What is the name for a saved snapshot in Git, with a message and a link to the snapshot before it?
hints: The word is also a verb: you do it when you save a state to the history.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A commit.

questions.onCorrect: A commit stores the snapshot, the message, the author, the time and the parent in one object.

misconceptions.feedback: Those words describe parts of the idea, but Git's own name for the saved state is different. It is also the verb used for saving one.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Git and GitHub is correct?
hints: One of them runs on your own computer with no account.
One of them is a company's website.

acceptedIdeas: Git is the program, and GitHub is a website that hosts repositories
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Git is the program, and GitHub is a website that hosts repositories

questions.onCorrect: Git runs on your computer, and GitHub, GitLab and others host copies of repositories on a website.

misconceptions.feedback: Git runs on your own computer with no account, so it cannot be the same thing as a company's website.
Look at which of the two runs on your own computer with no account.
A repository on your own disk is a full repository without any hosting service, so Git does not depend on one.

choices.label: Git is a program that only works through GitHub
Git and GitHub are two names for the same program
GitHub is the program, and Git is a website that hosts repositories

questions.prompt: Ana cloned a project of 450 commits and then made 2 new commits on her own laptop without pushing. How many commits does her repository hold?
hints: Start from what the clone gave her.
Her local commits are added to the history she already has.
Add the two new commits to the 450.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 450 from the clone plus 2 of her own: 450 + 2 = 452.

questions.onCorrect: Her two commits exist only in her repository until she pushes them, though the history is complete locally.

misconceptions.feedback: The clone gave her 450, and her two new commits are in her repository as well.
That counts only her new commits, and the clone's 450 are still there.

questions.prompt: A tracked file `a.txt` is edited, staged with `git add`, and then edited again. What does `git status --short` print for it?
hints: There are two separate differences: one between the index and the last commit, and one between the working tree and the index.
Both differences exist here, so both columns are filled.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: MM a.txt

questions.onCorrect: The first M is the staged version, which differs from the last commit, and the second M is the later edit that the index has never seen.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the state right after `git add`, before the second edit. The second edit adds an M in the right-hand column.
That is the state of an edit that was never staged. This file has been staged as well.
Two question marks mean untracked, and `a.txt` is already tracked.

choices.label: `MM a.txt`
` M a.txt`
`?? a.txt`
`M  a.txt`

questions.prompt: You create `notes.txt` in a project and never run `git add` on it. What word does Git use for a file like this?
hints: It appears with two question marks in `git status --short`.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Untracked.

questions.onCorrect: An untracked file stays out of every commit until you add it by name, even when you commit with `-a`.

misconceptions.feedback: A file can be new or unstaged and still be tracked. The word asked for describes a file Git has no record of.

questions.prompt: How many different versions of `a.txt` does Git hold at this moment, counting the working tree, the index and the last commit?
hints: Work out which version each place holds, using the lines above.
Compare them one by one: are any two of them equal?
Count the distinct version numbers.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The working tree holds version 3, the index holds version 2 and the last commit holds version 1, so 3.

questions.onCorrect: `git add` copies content as it is at that moment, so edits made afterwards need adding again.

misconceptions.feedback: The working tree differs from the index as well, because of the second edit. All three places differ.
Three places each hold their own content, and here none of them agrees with another.

questions.prompt: You changed five files, staged three of them and committed. How many files are still modified in the working tree and not committed?
hints: The commit contained only what was in the index.
Subtract the staged files from the changed files.
Five changed, three committed: what is left?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 5 changed files minus the 3 that were staged and committed leaves 2.

questions.onCorrect: Files you leave unstaged stay modified in the working tree, ready for a later commit of their own.

misconceptions.feedback: The three staged files were committed, so they no longer differ from the last commit.
Those three were the ones committed. The remaining files are the two left behind.

questions.prompt: You changed five files, staged three of them and committed. What happens to the other two files?
hints: The commit contained only what was in the index.
Ask what `git commit` does with files that were never added.

acceptedIdeas: They stay modified in the working tree, neither staged nor committed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They stay modified in the working tree, neither staged nor committed

questions.onCorrect: Files you leave unstaged stay modified in the working tree, ready for a later commit of their own.

misconceptions.feedback: A plain `git commit` records only what is in the index, and the two files were never added to it.
Leaving a file unstaged does not touch its content, so the edits are still in the working tree.
Git stages a file only when you run `git add` on it, so nothing is staged for the next commit unless you add it.

choices.label: They are discarded, because they were not staged
They are staged automatically, ready for the next commit
They are committed too, because `git commit` saves every modified file
They stay modified in the working tree, neither staged nor committed

questions.prompt: You have staged two files and left a third edited but unstaged. Which command, with one option added to its plain form, shows only the changes in the two staged files?
hints: Plain `git diff` compares the working tree with the index, so you need the other pair.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: git diff --cached (or --staged).

questions.onCorrect: `git diff --cached` compares the index with the last commit, which is exactly what `git commit` would record.

misconceptions.feedback: Plain `git diff` shows only the unstaged edits. An option on it switches to the staged ones.

questions.prompt: A tracked file `a.txt` has been edited, and a new file `new.txt` has never been added. You run `git commit -am` with a message. How many files does the new commit change?
hints: Ask which of the two files Git already tracks.
`commit -a` stages tracked files and ignores untracked ones.
Count only the tracked file that changed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: `git commit -a` stages tracked files only, so only `a.txt` is committed: 1 file.

questions.onCorrect: `new.txt` remains untracked after the commit, so a forgotten new file never sneaks in through `-a`, and has to be added by name.

misconceptions.feedback: `-a` adds changes to tracked files. `new.txt` is untracked, so it is left out.
`a.txt` is tracked and was edited, so it is committed.

questions.prompt: A tracked file `a.txt` has been edited, and a new file `new.txt` has never been added. You run `git commit -am` with a message. What does the new commit contain?
hints: Ask which of the two files Git already tracks.
`commit -a` stages tracked files and ignores untracked ones.

acceptedIdeas: The changes to `a.txt` only, with `new.txt` left out
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The changes to a.txt only, with new.txt left out

questions.onCorrect: `new.txt` remains untracked after the commit, so a forgotten new file never sneaks in through `-a`, and has to be added by name.

misconceptions.feedback: The `-a` option stages changes to tracked files only, and `new.txt` is untracked, so it is not included.
Git commits as usual when untracked files are present, leaving them out and listing them as untracked afterwards.
The `-a` option does not add `new.txt`, and `a.txt` is tracked, so its edit is in the commit.

choices.label: Nothing, because git refuses to commit while an untracked file exists
The changes to both `a.txt` and `new.txt`
The changes to `a.txt` only, with `new.txt` left out
The new file `new.txt` only, because it is the newer change

questions.prompt: A tracked file `b.txt` is edited, then staged with `git add b.txt`, then edited again. What does `git status --short` show for it?
hints: Compare the index with the last commit, then the working tree with the index.
Each of those two comparisons shows a difference here.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An M in both columns

questions.onCorrect: The left M is the staged edit and the right M is the edit made after staging.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what shows right after `git add`. The second edit added an M in the right-hand column.
A blank on the left means nothing is staged, but this file was staged before the second edit.
Two question marks mean untracked, and `b.txt` is a tracked file.

choices.label: An M in the left column only
An M in both columns
An M in the right column only
Two question marks

questions.prompt: A brand-new file `n.txt` has never been added. What does `git status --short` show for it?
hints: Git has no earlier version of the file to compare with.
The code for a file Git has no record of is not a letter.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Two question marks

questions.onCorrect: Git can compare nothing for a file it does not track, so it marks it with two question marks.

misconceptions.feedback: An A in the left column marks a new file that has already been staged. This one has not been added.
An M means a tracked file has changed, and Git has no earlier version of this file to compare.
That is a tracked file with a staged edit, and this file is not tracked.

choices.label: An A in the left column
An M in the right column
An M in the left column
Two question marks

questions.prompt: What does `git commit -a` leave out?
hints: The option stages files Git already knows about.
A new file is one Git does not know about yet.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: New, untracked files

questions.onCorrect: A new file has to be added by name once, and from then on it is tracked and `commit -a` includes its changes.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are exactly what `-a` stages.
Deleting a tracked file is a change to a tracked file, so `-a` includes it.
The message is given separately, with `-m`, and `-a` has nothing to do with it.

choices.label: Deleted tracked files
The commit message
New, untracked files
Changes to tracked files

questions.prompt: MD5, an older hashing function, produces 128 bits, and each hexadecimal character carries 4 bits. How many characters does a full MD5 hash have?
hints: Divide the total number of bits by the bits each character carries.
Write the result as a plain number of characters.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 128 bits ÷ 4 bits per character = 32 characters.

questions.onCorrect: Seven characters are usually enough to name one commit, because they are chosen from 16 symbols and so give 16 to the 7th power possibilities.

misconceptions.feedback: 128 is the number of bits. Each hexadecimal character carries 4 of them.
That would be 8 bits per character, but one hexadecimal character carries 4.

questions.prompt: Which Git object type lists names with the hashes of the files or sub-folders they refer to?
hints: It represents a folder, as the blob represents a file.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A tree.

questions.onCorrect: A blob stores only the contents of a file, so the name and the folder structure live in the tree above it.

misconceptions.feedback: A blob holds a file's contents and has no name inside it. The names live in the object above it.
A commit points to one of these. The list of names lives in the object it points to.

questions.prompt: A project has d1/x and d2/y, both containing the same text, and you commit it. How many objects does Git create in total, counting blobs, trees and the commit?
hints: Count the blobs first: identical contents are stored once.
The two folders hold entries with different names, so they are different trees, and the root is another.
1 blob, then trees, then the commit.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1 blob + 3 trees (d1, d2 and the root) + 1 commit = 5 objects.

questions.onCorrect: `git count-objects` confirms this count in a real repository, which reports 5 loose objects for such a commit.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts two blobs, but identical content is stored once, so there is only one.
That leaves out the root tree, which lists d1 and d2.
That counts the blob and the commit only. The folders are trees too.

questions.prompt: Three files are committed. d1/x and d2/y both contain same, and z contains other. How many blob objects does Git store?
hints: A blob is named by its content alone.
Two files with identical content share one blob.
Count the distinct contents.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: same is stored once and other is stored once: 2 blobs.

questions.onCorrect: A blob has no file name inside it, so unrelated files with the same text share one stored object.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts each file separately, but identical content has one hash and so one blob.
The file z holds different text and gets a blob of its own.

questions.prompt: A project has eight commits in a line. You edit the message of commit 2. How many commits have a different hash afterwards?
hints: The edit changes commit 2's content, so its hash changes.
Each later commit contains its parent's hash.
Count commits 2 to 8 inclusive.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Commit 2 changes, and commits 3 to 8 each contain their parent's changed hash: 7 commits in all.

questions.onCorrect: Commit 1 does not contain anything that changed, so it keeps its hash.

misconceptions.feedback: The edited commit changes, and so does every commit that has it as an ancestor.
That counts commits 3 to 8 only, and commit 2 itself has a new hash too.
Commit 1 is before the edit and contains nothing that changed, so it keeps its hash.

questions.prompt: A project has eight commits in a line. You edit the message of commit 2. Which commits have a different hash afterwards?
hints: The edit changes commit 2's content, so its hash changes.
Each commit contains the hash of its parent. Ask what that means for the commit that follows one whose hash has changed.

acceptedIdeas: Commit 2 and every commit after it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Commit 2 and every commit after it

questions.onCorrect: Commit 1 does not contain anything that changed, so it keeps its hash, while every commit from 2 onwards has a new one.

misconceptions.feedback: Only commit 2's own content was edited, but every later commit records the hash of the commit before it. Ask what that does to commit 3.
A commit records its parent's hash and not its child's, so commit 1 contains nothing that changed and keeps its hash.
Commit 1 comes before the edit and contains nothing that changed, so it keeps its hash.

choices.label: All eight commits
Commit 2 and every commit after it
Only commit 2, because it is the only one that was edited
Commit 2 and the commit before it

questions.prompt: A teammate has your commit 6. You rewrite commit 4 on your copy. What do you both now have?
hints: The new commit 4 has a different hash, and the later commits record the parent's hash.
Which commits come before the edit?

acceptedIdeas: The same commits 1 to 3, but different commits 4 to 6
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The same commits 1 to 3, but different commits 4 to 6

questions.onCorrect: Commits 1 to 3 are shared, and the rewritten commits 4 to 6 are new objects, so the two histories have diverged after commit 3.

misconceptions.feedback: A commit's hash covers its parent's hash as well as its own files, so a changed parent changes it.
Both repositories are valid. They simply no longer agree beyond the shared start.
The earliest commits come before the edit and are untouched, so they keep their hashes.

choices.label: The same commits 1 to 3, but different commits 4 to 6
The same history, because commit 6 itself was not edited
Different commits 1 to 6, all with new hashes
A broken repository that Git refuses to open

questions.prompt: A SHA-256 hash is 256 bits. Writing each hexadecimal character as 4 bits, how many characters does a full SHA-256 hash have?
hints: Each hexadecimal character carries 4 bits.
Divide the total number of bits by the bits per character.
Do the division as a plain calculation.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 256 ÷ 4 = 64 characters.

questions.onCorrect: SHA-256 hashes are 64 characters, which is why repositories using them cannot mix with 40-character SHA-1 repositories.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of bits, and each character carries 4.
That would be 8 bits per character, but one hexadecimal character carries 4.

questions.prompt: Two files in different folders contain exactly the same text. How many blob objects does Git store for them?
hints: A blob is named by the hash of its content.
Same content gives the same name.
Count how many distinct names there are.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Identical content has one hash, so Git stores 1 blob.

questions.onCorrect: The two folders' trees each list the same blob under their own file name.

misconceptions.feedback: Each file has its own entry in a tree, but the content behind both is a single blob.

questions.prompt: A history has five commits in a line, and you change the message of commit 3. How many commits get a new hash?
hints: The edited commit changes, and every later one contains its parent's hash.
Commits before the edit are untouched.
Count the edited commit and everything after it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Commits 3, 4 and 5 change: 3 commits.

questions.onCorrect: Commits 1 and 2 are before the change, so they keep their old hashes.

misconceptions.feedback: The later commits contain their parent's hash, so they change as well.
Those are the commits that do not change. The edit and everything after it do.
Commits 1 and 2 are before the edit and are unaffected.

questions.prompt: A project has seven commits in a line, C1 oldest and C7 newest, and HEAD is C7. Which commit is HEAD~2?
hints: HEAD~1 is the parent of HEAD.
questions.onCorrect: Each ~ is one step along the parent links, so two steps back from C7 reaches C5.

misconceptions.feedback: The tilde counts steps back from HEAD, and not from the oldest commit.

questions.prompt: Git names a commit by counting parent links back from HEAD, so HEAD~1 is the parent of HEAD. A project has seven commits in a line, C1 oldest and C7 newest, and HEAD is C7. Which commit is HEAD~2?
hints: HEAD~1 is the parent of HEAD.
For HEAD~2, take one more step back along the parent links.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: C5

questions.onCorrect: Each ~ is one step along the parent links, so two steps back from C7 reaches C5.

misconceptions.feedback: The number after the tilde counts steps back from HEAD, and not forward from the oldest commit.
C6 is the parent of HEAD, which is HEAD~1. HEAD~2 is one step further back.
HEAD alone names C7. The number after the tilde says how many parent links to follow from it.

choices.label: C2
C6
C5
C7

questions.prompt: Eight commits C1 to C8 are in a line and HEAD is C8. HEAD~3 is which commit? Give its number.
hints: Count steps back along the parent links.
HEAD itself is the newest commit.
Subtract the steps from the newest commit's number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three steps back from C8 is C5: 8 − 3 = 5.

questions.onCorrect: HEAD~0 would be HEAD itself, and the numbering of commits in the figure is only a label, since Git names commits by hash.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts forward from the oldest. The tilde counts back from HEAD.
That is HEAD~4, not HEAD~3.
That is HEAD~2, which is two steps back.

questions.prompt: main holds c1 to c5, and feature was started after c2 and holds c1, c2, f1 and f2. How many commits are in feature..main?
hints: The range keeps what main reaches that feature does not.
The shared commits are the ones before the branch point.
Remove the shared commits from main's list and count the rest.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: main reaches c1 to c5 and feature reaches c1, c2, f1 and f2. Removing the shared c1 and c2 leaves c3, c4 and c5: 3 commits.

questions.onCorrect: The reverse range, main..feature, would hold f1 and f2, so the two orders give different questions.

misconceptions.feedback: That is main..feature, the commits on feature that main lacks. The range asked for is the other way round.
That counts everything main reaches, including the shared commits.

questions.prompt: main holds c1 to c4, and feature holds c1, c2, f1, f2, f3 and f4. How many commits are in main..feature?
hints: List what each branch reaches, then cross out the shared ones.
Only the commits that feature has and main lacks stay in the range.
Count the ones that remain.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: feature reaches f1 to f4 beyond the shared c1 and c2, so main..feature holds 4 commits.

questions.onCorrect: The reverse range, feature..main, would hold c3 and c4.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts everything feature reaches, including the shared commits.
That is feature..main, which is the opposite question.

questions.prompt: A line in `config.py` looks wrong, and you want to see, beside every line of the file, the commit that last changed it. Which Git command does that?
hints: The command is named after what you do when you look for who made a change.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: git blame.

questions.onCorrect: `git blame` names a commit for each line, and the commit's message and its diff then say why.

misconceptions.feedback: Those show commits or differences, but none of them annotates a file line by line.

questions.prompt: On `feature`, which holds f1 and shares c1 and c2 with `main`, `git log --oneline` is run. How many commits does it list?
hints: Follow the parent links from f1 all the way back.
Commits before the branch point are reachable too.
Count f1 and its ancestors.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: `git log` lists all commits reachable from feature: f1, c2 and c1, which is 3.

questions.onCorrect: The commit c3 is not listed, because feature cannot reach it by following parent links.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the branch's own commit. The shared earlier commits are reachable from it too.
c3 lives on main only, and feature cannot reach it.

questions.prompt: `main` holds c1, c2 and c3. `feature` started after c2 and holds c1, c2 and f1. You are on `feature` and run `git log --oneline`. Which commits does it list?
hints: Follow the parent links from f1 all the way back.
Commits before the branch point are reachable from f1 too.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: f1, c2 and c1

questions.onCorrect: The commit c3 is not listed, because feature cannot reach it by following parent links.

misconceptions.feedback: The commits on feature that main lacks are what main..feature selects, whereas `git log` lists everything reachable from where you are, including the commits before the branch point.
`git log` lists the commits reachable from the one you are on, and c3 is not among them, because feature cannot reach it by following parent links.
`git log` follows the parent links from the commit you are on, which here is f1, and does not switch to another branch.

choices.label: f1 only, because it is the only commit that feature has and main lacks
c3, c2 and c1, because `git log` lists the main branch
f1, c2, c1 and c3, because `git log` lists every commit in the repository
f1, c2 and c1

questions.prompt: A straight history has commits C1 (oldest) to C5, and HEAD is C5. HEAD~2 is which commit? Give its number.
hints: Count back from the newest commit along the parent links.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two steps back from C5 is C3: 5 − 2 = 3.

questions.onCorrect: HEAD~2 is two parent links back from C5, which is C3.

misconceptions.feedback: C4 is HEAD~1, one step back. HEAD~2 is one step further.
The number after the tilde counts back from HEAD and not forward from the oldest commit.

questions.prompt: main holds c1, c2 and c3. feature branched after c2 and holds c1, c2 and f1. How many commits are in main..feature?
hints: List what each branch reaches.
Remove the commits both branches reach.
Count what remains of the first list.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: feature reaches f1 beyond the shared c1 and c2, so main..feature holds 1 commit.

questions.onCorrect: feature..main holds exactly 1 commit as well, c3, but it is a different one.

misconceptions.feedback: c1 and c2 are shared, so they are excluded from the range.
That counts everything feature reaches, but the shared commits are excluded.

questions.prompt: Which command prints one commit's message together with the change it made?
hints: The answer takes a commit name and displays the commit itself.
The two diff-like options compare states, and do not display a commit's message.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `git show`

questions.onCorrect: `git show` prints the message, the author and the diff for the commit you name, and defaults to HEAD.

misconceptions.feedback: `git blame` annotates a file's lines with the commit that last changed each. It does not display one commit's change.
That compares the index with the last commit and shows no message.
`git status` lists what differs between the three places and shows no commit's content.

choices.label: `git show`
`git status`
`git blame`
`git diff --cached`

questions.prompt: main points at c3. After `git branch x`, how many branch names point at c3?
hints: `git branch x` puts a new label on the commit you are on.
The existing label does not move.
Count the labels on c3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: main still points at c3 and x now does too: 2 names.

questions.onCorrect: A commit can carry any number of labels, and creating one copies no files.

misconceptions.feedback: The old label stays where it was, and the new one is added to the same commit.
`git branch x` creates a label on the current commit, and main stays there.

questions.prompt: main points at c3 and HEAD is on main. You run `git branch x`. What is true afterwards?
hints: `git branch x` puts a new label on the commit you are on.
The existing label does not move, and neither does HEAD.

acceptedIdeas: Both main and x point at c3, and HEAD is still on main
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both main and x point at c3, and HEAD is still on main

questions.onCorrect: A commit can carry any number of labels, and creating one copies no files.

misconceptions.feedback: Creating a branch copies no files. It adds one new name that points at the commit you are on.
`git branch x` makes no commit, so there is no new commit for x to point at.
`git branch` only creates the name. HEAD stays on main until you run `git switch x`.

choices.label: Both main and x point at c3, and HEAD is still on main
Both main and x point at c3, and HEAD is now on x
x is a copy of the project, and main is unchanged

questions.prompt: What is the name of the file in .git that records which branch you are on?
hints: It is the same name as the label in the figure that moves when you switch.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: HEAD.

questions.onCorrect: HEAD usually holds a line such as ref: refs/heads/main, naming the branch, and holds a bare hash when detached.

misconceptions.feedback: main is a branch, and the file named is the one that says which branch you are on.

questions.prompt: The session started from a history of c1, c2 and c3 in a line. At the end, how many commits can be reached from x, counting the commit x points at?
hints: Follow the parent links from c4 back to the start.
List every commit you pass through, including c4.
Count the list.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: c4, c3, c2 and c1 are reachable: 4 commits.

questions.onCorrect: c5 is not reachable from x, because it lives on main only.

misconceptions.feedback: c4 itself counts, and the history reaches back to its first commit.
c5 was made on main, and x cannot reach it.

questions.prompt: You make two commits in a detached HEAD state, then switch to main. How many branch names point at the newer of those two commits?

questions.prompt: You check out an old commit directly, so that HEAD points at it with no branch, make two commits, and then switch to main. What points at the newer of your two commits?
hints: A commit made while HEAD is detached moves only HEAD.
Switching away leaves the commits behind.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No branch name at all

questions.onCorrect: Without a name the commits are easy to lose, and the reflog is the usual way back, as a later lesson shows.

misconceptions.feedback: Switching to main moves HEAD to main's commit and leaves main where it was, so main does not carry the new commits along.

choices.label: main, which moves forward to take them with it
No branch name at all

questions.prompt: You are in a detached HEAD state with a commit you want to keep. What does `git switch -c rescue` do?
hints: The command creates something and switches to it.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Creates a branch called rescue at the current commit and attaches HEAD to it

questions.onCorrect: A branch named at the current commit keeps those commits reachable once you leave.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing is deleted. The command adds a name.
Git does not copy files for a branch. A branch is a pointer.
main is untouched. A new branch is created instead.

Copies the working tree into a new folder called rescue

questions.prompt: In a SHA-256 repository a hash is 64 characters, and a branch file holds the hash and one newline. How many bytes is .git/refs/heads/main?
hints: A ref file holds the hash and a newline, one byte each per character.
The SHA-1 version of the file is 40 plus the newline.
Add the newline to the length of the hash.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 64 characters for the hash plus one for the newline: 65 bytes.

questions.onCorrect: The same arithmetic gives 41 bytes for SHA-1.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the hash alone. The newline adds one more byte.
That is the size with a 40-character SHA-1 hash.

questions.prompt: How many bytes is the file .git/refs/heads/main, which holds a 40-character hash and a newline?
hints: Each character is one byte here.
The file holds the hash and a newline.
Add the newline to the length of the hash.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 40 characters plus 1 newline is 41 bytes.

misconceptions.feedback: The newline at the end of the line is a byte as well.

questions.prompt: What does the command `git branch x` create?
hints: Think about what the command stores.
Ask whether a branch needs a snapshot and a message, as a commit does.

acceptedIdeas: A new name that points at the commit you are on

questions.onCorrect: The new branch shares all history with the branch it was created from, until someone commits to it.

misconceptions.feedback: A commit needs a snapshot and a message made at the moment you commit. This command only stores a name and a hash.
Git does not copy files for a branch. A branch is a pointer.
No commit is made, and a commit would hold the whole project in any case.

A new commit with the same message as the current one
A copy of the project's files in a new folder

questions.prompt: You run `git branch x`, then `git switch x`, and then make a commit. Which branch name now points at the new commit?
hints: A commit moves the branch HEAD is attached to.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: x.

questions.onCorrect: main stays where it was, and x moves forward by one commit.

misconceptions.feedback: HEAD was on x after the switch, so the commit advanced x and left main alone.

questions.prompt: main ends at c2 and feature holds c1, c2 and f1. How many new commits does `git merge feature` create on main?
hints: Is main's tip an ancestor of feature's tip?
If so, main's label can simply move forward.
Count the commits Git has to create to move a label.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: main's tip is an ancestor of feature's tip, so Git fast-forwards and creates no commit: 0.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Revert adds one commit that reverses B and removes none: 3 + 1 = 4.

questions.onCorrect: The original B stays in the history next to its revert.

hints: Revert never deletes a commit.

misconceptions.feedback: Removing B from the history would be a rewrite, which is what revert avoids. B stays where it is.

choices.label: A and C, with B removed from the history

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count after the first reset. The second moved the branch forward again.

questions.prompt: A branch has commits `one`, `two` and `three`. You run `git reset --hard HEAD~2` and then `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}`. What does the branch hold afterwards?
hints: `HEAD@{1}` names where HEAD was one move ago.

questions.onCorrect: Because the reflog kept the position, the `reset --hard` cost nothing here.

misconceptions.feedback: The reflog still records where HEAD was before the first reset, so the commits were not lost, and `HEAD@{1}` names commit `three`.

misconceptions.feedback: 2 to the 12th power is 4,096, which falls short of 5,000.

Add the tests made to the one still needed.

misconceptions.feedback: Bisect runs each test once and believes the result.
It makes no difference to the speed, and it spoils the answer.
Bisect starts regardless. The harm shows up in the commit it reports.

It makes the search faster
Nothing, because bisect repeats each test
It may send the search into the wrong half and give a wrong commit

questions.prompt: A history of 1,000 commits grows to 2,000. How many extra tests, at most, does bisect need for the longer history?
hints: Doubling the history adds one halving.
Compare the smallest powers of two that reach each size.
Subtract the smaller number of tests from the larger.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1,000 needs 10 tests and 2,000 needs 11, because 2^11 = 2,048 reaches 2,000: 1 extra test.

questions.onCorrect: A thousandfold increase adds ten tests, as the table shows.

misconceptions.feedback: Bisect does not need a test per extra commit, since each test halves the range.

questions.prompt: What is the largest number of tests bisect needs for 1,000 commits?
hints: Find the smallest power of two that reaches 1,000.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many commits remain after the first test, not the number of tests.

hints: A thousand commits need ten tests.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2^19 = 524,288 is too few and 2^20 = 1,048,576 is enough: 20 tests.

questions.onCorrect: A test per commit would be a million tests, so bisect saves almost all of the work.

misconceptions.feedback: 2 to the 19th power is 524,288, which falls short of a million.
That is how many commits remain after one test.

questions.prompt: Which command finds commits that added or removed a given string?

questions.prompt: Bob pushed two commits and Alice has run no Git command since. How many commits does her origin/main have that her main lacks?
