questions.onCorrect: The fix and the feature leave the major number as it was.

misconceptions.feedback: A breaking change raises the major number, so it ends higher than the start.
A breaking change adds one to the major number, not two.

questions.prompt: Which commit message will help someone reading the log a year from now?
hints: The reader can see which lines changed in the diff.
What would they still need to learn?

acceptedIdeas: Cache user lookups, which took 300 ms and ran on every page
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Cache user lookups, which took 300 ms and ran on every page

questions.onCorrect: A summary with a reason tells the reader what the change was for, which the diff cannot say.

misconceptions.feedback: That says how the change works, which the diff already shows. The message should add what the diff cannot.
A reader a year from now will not have the meeting, and the message does not say what was wrong.
The diff already shows which line changed, and line numbers move. The message should give the reason.

choices.label: Add a dictionary in `cache.py` that stores each user lookup
Update the lookup code, as agreed in yesterday's meeting
Cache user lookups, which took 300 ms and ran on every page
Change line 42 of `cache.py` to fix the slow pages

questions.prompt: With `*.log` in `.gitignore`, you create three new files ending in `.log`. How many of them does `git status --short` list as untracked?
hints: Ignore patterns hide matching untracked files.
The files match the pattern.
Count how many Git lists.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ignored files are hidden from the untracked list: 0.

questions.onCorrect: A file that matches a pattern but was already tracked would still show when edited.

misconceptions.feedback: The pattern matches all of them, so Git does not list any.
Each file matches the pattern, so none is listed.

questions.prompt: The pattern `*.log` is in `.gitignore`, and you create three new files ending in `.log`. What does `git status --short` show for them?
hints: Ignore patterns hide matching untracked files.
The new files match the pattern.

acceptedIdeas: Nothing, because Git treats files that match the pattern as invisible
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Nothing, because Git treats files that match the pattern as invisible

questions.onCorrect: A file that matches a pattern but was already tracked would still show when edited.

misconceptions.feedback: A new file is listed as untracked only if no ignore pattern matches it, and these files match `*.log`.
The pattern applies from the start. A new file that matches it is never listed as untracked, whether or not you run `git add` on it.

choices.label: ?? for all three until you run `git add`, and nothing afterwards
Nothing, because Git treats files that match the pattern as invisible
?? for all three, because a new file is always untracked

questions.prompt: A password was committed and pushed, then deleted in the next commit. Replacing an exposed password with a new one, so that the old one stops working, has a standard name. What is the one word?
hints: The old value is still in the earlier commit and in every clone, so the secret itself has to be replaced.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: rotate

questions.onCorrect: Rewriting history can remove the commit from the host, but copies may already exist, so the old password has to stop working.

misconceptions.feedback: Deleting it in a later commit leaves it in the history, and `.gitignore` does not affect a committed file. The question asks for the word used when the password is replaced.
Those describe the right action, but the standard word for replacing an exposed secret is a different one.

questions.prompt: The version is 2.4.1 and you add a backwards-compatible feature. What is the new version?
hints: A compatible feature raises the middle number.
The last number resets to zero.
questions.onCorrect: A minor bump tells users that the release adds something and breaks nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the bump for a bug fix. A new feature raises the minor number.
That is for a breaking change.

questions.prompt: The version is 2.4.1 and you make a breaking change. What is the new version?
hints: A breaking change raises the first number.
The other two return to zero.
questions.onCorrect: A major bump warns users that upgrading may need changes on their side.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the bump for a compatible feature. A breaking change raises the major number.
That is the bump for a bug fix.

questions.prompt: A password was committed and pushed, then deleted in the next commit. What should be done?
hints: The old commit still holds the password.
Anyone who cloned the project has it.

acceptedIdeas: Treat it as exposed and change the password
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Treat it as exposed and change the password

questions.onCorrect: A pushed secret stays in the history and in every clone, so the only safe fix is to make the old value useless.

misconceptions.feedback: The earlier commit and every clone still hold it.
An ignore rule affects untracked files, and the password is already in the history.
Rewriting the history can remove the commit from the host, but copies may already exist, so the old password still has to stop working.

choices.label: Treat it as exposed and change the password
Add it to .gitignore
Nothing, because it is deleted
Rewrite the history and consider the problem solved

questions.prompt: A project has 200 files. You edit three of them and commit. What does the new commit's snapshot contain?
hints: Think of a commit as a photograph of the project.
A photograph shows everything in the project, not just what moved.

acceptedIdeas: All 200 files, as they are after your edits
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: All 200 files, as they are after your edits

questions.onCorrect: Git reuses the 197 unchanged files from the previous commit, so storing the full snapshot costs very little extra space.

choices.label: Only the three files that changed
Only the changed lines in those three files
All 200 files, as they are after your edits
The three changed files, with the other 197 left in the earlier commit

misconceptions.feedback: The 197 files you did not touch are in the snapshot as well, along with the three you changed.
A commit is a snapshot of the whole project, so it holds every file and not just the lines that changed.
Git does reuse files from the earlier commit when it stores the new one, but that is a matter of storage. The snapshot you can look at is a complete project.

questions.prompt: Ben has cloned a project, and then his network connection drops. Which of these needs the network?
hints: Ask which of these actions reaches another machine.
Everything in a clone's history is already on its own disk.

acceptedIdeas: Sending a new commit to the hosting service
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sending a new commit to the hosting service

questions.onCorrect: Only pushing and fetching reach the other machine. Reading history, comparing commits and committing all work on the local copy.

choices.label: Making a new commit
Sending a new commit to the hosting service
Reading the message of the very first commit
Comparing two old commits

misconceptions.feedback: A commit is written to the repository on Ben's own disk, so it needs no connection.
The clone downloaded every commit back to the first one, so old commits can be read from his own disk.
Both commits are already in his clone, and comparing them is done on his own machine.

questions.prompt: A tracked file `a.txt` is edited and staged with `git add a.txt`. It is then edited again and staged a second time with `git add a.txt`. What does `git status --short` show for it?
hints: There are two comparisons: the index against the last commit, and the working tree against the index.
Ask what the second `git add` did to the index.

acceptedIdeas: An M in the left column only
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An M in the left column only

questions.onCorrect: Each `git add` copies the file as it is at that moment, so the second one brought the index up to date with the latest edit.

choices.label: An M in both columns
An M in the right column only
An M in the left column only
Two question marks

misconceptions.feedback: An M on the right would mean the working tree still differs from the index. The second `git add` copied the latest edit into the index, so the two now agree.
A blank on the left means nothing is staged, but this file was added, so the index differs from the last commit.
Two question marks mean untracked, and `a.txt` is already tracked.

questions.prompt: You edit `a.txt` and `b.txt`, stage only `a.txt` with `git add a.txt`, and run `git commit -m "fix"`. Which version of `b.txt` is in the new commit?
hints: A commit records the index.
Ask what the index holds for a file that was never added.

acceptedIdeas: The version from before your edit, as it was in the last commit
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The version from before your edit, as it was in the last commit

questions.onCorrect: Your edit to `b.txt` is still in the working tree, waiting for a commit of its own.

choices.label: The version from before your edit, as it was in the last commit
The version with your edit, because the commit saves the whole working tree
No version, because `b.txt` is left out of the commit's snapshot
Git asks which version to use before it commits

misconceptions.feedback: A commit is built from the index, not the working tree. `b.txt` was never added, so the index still held its earlier version.
A snapshot holds every file in the project, including the files you did not stage.
Git does not ask. It commits whatever the index holds and leaves the rest of the working tree alone.

questions.prompt: A SHA-512 hash is 512 bits long. Writing each hexadecimal character as 4 bits, how many characters does a full SHA-512 hash have?
hints: Each hexadecimal character carries 4 bits.
Divide the total number of bits by the bits per character.
Do the division as a plain calculation.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 512 ÷ 4 = 128 characters.

questions.onCorrect: A SHA-512 hash is twice as long as a SHA-256 hash of 64 characters, because it carries twice as many bits.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of bits, and each hexadecimal character carries 4 of them.
That is the length of a SHA-256 hash, which has 256 bits. A SHA-512 hash has twice as many bits.

questions.prompt: A history has six commits in a line, and you change the message of commit 3. How many commits get a new hash?
hints: The edited commit changes, and every later one contains its parent's hash.
Commits before the edit are untouched.
Count the edited commit and everything after it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Commits 3, 4, 5 and 6 change: 4 commits.

questions.onCorrect: Commits 1 and 2 are before the change, so they keep their old hashes.

misconceptions.feedback: The later commits contain their parent's hash, so they change as well.
Those are the commits that keep their hashes. The edit and everything after it change.
Commits 1 and 2 come before the edit and are unaffected.

questions.prompt: main holds c1 to c7. feature branched after c5 and holds c1 to c5, f1, f2 and f3. How many commits are in feature..main?
hints: The range keeps what main reaches that feature does not.
The shared commits are the ones before the branch point.
Remove the shared commits from main's list and count the rest.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: main reaches c1 to c7 and feature reaches c1 to c5 and f1 to f3. Removing the shared c1 to c5 leaves c6 and c7: 2 commits.

questions.onCorrect: The reverse range, main..feature, would hold f1, f2 and f3, so the order of the two names matters.

misconceptions.feedback: That is main..feature, the commits feature has and main lacks. The range asked for is the other way round.
That counts everything main reaches, including the shared commits.
Those are the shared commits, which both branches reach and which the range leaves out.

questions.prompt: HEAD is attached to the branch `x`, and you make a commit. Which file inside `.git` now holds a different commit hash?
hints: A commit moves the branch HEAD is attached to.
Each branch is a small file that holds a commit hash.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `.git/refs/heads/x`

questions.onCorrect: The file for x now holds the new commit's hash, while `.git/HEAD` still names x and the file for main is untouched.

choices.label: `.git/HEAD`
`.git/refs/heads/main`
`.git/refs/heads/x`

misconceptions.feedback: While HEAD is attached to a branch, `.git/HEAD` holds a line naming that branch, and a commit does not change it.
A commit moves only the branch that HEAD is attached to, and HEAD is attached to `x`, not `main`.

questions.prompt: Branch `x` points at c4, `main` points at c3, and HEAD is on `x`. You run `git switch main` and then make a commit c5. Which branch label moves to c5?
hints: After `git switch main`, ask which branch HEAD is attached to.
A commit moves the branch HEAD is attached to.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only `main`

questions.onCorrect: Now main is at c5 and x is at c4, so the two branches have diverged from c3.

choices.label: Both `main` and `x`
Only `x`
Neither of them
Only `main`

misconceptions.feedback: A commit moves only the branch HEAD is attached to, so one label moves and not two.
`x` is where HEAD was before the switch. `git switch main` moved HEAD off it, so `x` stays at c4.
After the switch HEAD is attached to a branch, and a commit always moves the branch HEAD is attached to.

questions.prompt: You make a commit d2 with a detached HEAD, run `git switch -c keep`, and then run `git switch main`. What points at d2 now?
hints: `git switch -c keep` creates a branch at the commit you are on.
A branch stays where it was put when HEAD moves away.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The branch `keep`

questions.onCorrect: A branch named at d2 keeps it reachable once you leave, which is why the name is created before switching away.

choices.label: The branch `keep`
Nothing, because switching to `main` leaves d2 behind
`main`, which moved forward to d2
HEAD, which stays on d2

misconceptions.feedback: That is what happens without the new branch. `git switch -c keep` gave d2 a name before you left, and the name stays where it was put.
Switching to `main` moves HEAD onto main's commit and leaves main where it was.
The switch to `main` moved HEAD off d2.

questions.prompt: A repository has five branches. Each branch file holds a 40-character hash and a newline, one byte for each character. How many bytes do the five files hold in total?
hints: Work out the size of one branch file first.
Each file holds the hash and a newline.
Multiply by the number of branches.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each file is 40 + 1 = 41 bytes, and 5 × 41 = 205 bytes.

questions.onCorrect: Each branch is only a tiny file like this, which is why creating one is instant.

misconceptions.feedback: Each file also holds a newline after the hash, which is one more byte per file.
That is the size of a single branch file.
That adds the five newlines to a single hash. Every file holds its own hash.

questions.prompt: You run `git switch main`, then `git branch y`, and then make a commit. Which branch name now points at the new commit?
hints: A commit moves the branch HEAD is attached to.
Ask whether `git branch y` changed where HEAD is.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only `main`

questions.onCorrect: `y` is created at the same commit as `main`, and then `main` moves on alone.

choices.label: Only `y`
Only `main`
Both `main` and `y`
Neither of them

misconceptions.feedback: `git branch y` creates the name but does not move HEAD. Ask which branch HEAD is still attached to.
A commit moves only the branch HEAD is attached to, so one label moves and not two.
HEAD is attached to a branch here, and a commit always moves that branch.

questions.prompt: A file has six lines. On `main`, lines 1 and 2 are edited, and on `feature`, line 5 is edited. After you merge `feature` into `main`, how many lines of the merged file differ from the base version?
hints: Each line was changed by only one side.
Git keeps a change when the other side left the line alone.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The edits do not touch, so Git keeps both sides' changes: 2 lines from main plus 1 line from feature is 3 lines.

questions.onCorrect: Changes that do not overlap or touch merge with no conflict, and the next lesson shows when that stops being true.

misconceptions.feedback: That keeps only main's edits. Line 5 was changed by feature alone, so Git keeps that change too.
That keeps only feature's edit. Lines 1 and 2 were changed by main alone, so they stay changed.
A conflict needs overlapping or neighbouring edits. Two unchanged lines separate main's edits from feature's, so Git combines them without asking.

questions.prompt: Why does `f` need `git add f` before `git commit` can finish the merge?
hints: After the merge stops, `git status --short` lists `f` as `UU`.
Ask what changes that status.

acceptedIdeas: To tell Git that the conflict in `f` is resolved
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: To tell Git that the conflict in `f` is resolved

questions.onCorrect: Until `f` is added it stays listed as unmerged, and a commit cannot finish the merge while any file is.

choices.label: To tell Git that the conflict in `f` is resolved
To remove the marker lines from `f`
To choose which branch's version of `f` wins
To send the merged `f` to the hosting service

misconceptions.feedback: `git add` copies the file as it stands, markers included. Removing the markers is the editing done before it.
The choice of text was made when you edited `f`. `git add` takes the file as you left it.
Sending commits to a host is `git push`, and `git add` works inside your own repository.

questions.prompt: A base file has six lines. One branch edits line 3 and the other edits line 5. What does the merge do?
hints: An unchanged line lies between the edits.
Do the edits touch?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Merges cleanly

questions.onCorrect: Each side's change is kept, since the other side left that line alone.

choices.label: Reports a conflict
Merges cleanly
Keeps only one edit
Refuses to run

misconceptions.feedback: Conflicts need overlapping or neighbouring edits, and an unchanged line lies between these two.
Both changes are kept, since neither disturbs the other.
A merge always runs. It may stop part-way at a conflict, and there is none here.

questions.prompt: One branch edits line 4 and the other edits line 5 of a six-line file. What does Git report?
hints: The lines differ, but do they touch?
Git merges changes in hunks, not single lines.

acceptedIdeas: A conflict, because the two edits touch
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A conflict, because the two edits touch

questions.onCorrect: Adjacent changes count as one place, so Git asks a person to decide.

choices.label: A clean merge, because the two lines are different
A clean merge that keeps only the later edit
A conflict, because the two edits touch
An error, because the base file has changed

misconceptions.feedback: The lines differ, but neighbouring edits still count as one place.
A merge never silently drops one side's edit. Edits that touch are left for a person to decide.
The base is found as usual. The disagreement is in the text.

questions.prompt: You have five commits on a branch, and a teammate has pulled all five. You run `git rebase -i HEAD~2`, reword both of the last two commits, and force-push. How many of your teammate's five commits are still in your branch?
hints: Compare hashes, not messages.
A rewrite changes the commits from the first edited line onward.
Count the commits before that point.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Rewording replaces the last two commits with copies that have new hashes. The first three commits are not replayed and keep their hashes, so 3 of the five are still in the branch.

questions.onCorrect: Your teammate's last two commits differ from yours, and they have to reconcile the difference.

misconceptions.feedback: Only the commits from the first edited line onward are replaced. The three before them keep their hashes.
That is the number of commits you rewrote. The ones before them were not touched.
Rewording gives a commit a new hash, and so it gives the commit after it a new hash too.

questions.prompt: In the list that `git rebase -i HEAD~3` opens, a typo fix sits below the commit it belongs with. Which word do you put in front of the typo fix to fold it into the commit above?
hints: Think about which word combines a commit's change into the one above it.
The other words keep the commit separate, change only its message, or remove it.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `squash`

questions.onCorrect: Squashing folds the typo fix into the commit above, so two commits become one, and every commit from that line onward gets a new hash.

choices.label: `squash`
`reword`
`pick`
`drop`

misconceptions.feedback: `reword` keeps the commit separate and only lets you rewrite its message.
`pick` keeps the commit exactly as it is, so the typo fix would stay a separate commit.
`drop` removes the commit and its change completely, so the typo fix would be lost.

questions.prompt: base is shared. feat has 3 commits and main has 2 more since base. After `git rebase main` on feat, which of these ranges is empty?
hints: A..B holds what B has that A lacks.
After the rebase, feat sits on top of main's tip.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `feat..main`

questions.onCorrect: feat holds everything main has, plus its own three replayed commits, so only main..feat has anything in it.

choices.label: `main..feat`
`feat..main`
Both of them
Neither of them

misconceptions.feedback: `main..feat` holds what feat has and main lacks, which is the three replayed commits.
Only one is empty. feat now holds three commits that main lacks.
After the rebase feat contains every commit that main has, so one of the two ranges has nothing in it.

questions.prompt: Commit `two` is gone from the branch, and the reflog lists it as `HEAD@{1}`. Which command moves the branch forward to that commit again?
hints: Ask which command moves a branch to a commit you name.
One of these only lists positions, and another adds a new commit.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `git reset --hard`

questions.onCorrect: The branch is back at `two` and `two.txt` returns, because the reflog kept the commit reachable by name.

choices.label: `git restore`
`git reset --hard`
`git revert`
`git reflog`

misconceptions.feedback: `git restore` puts files in the working tree back to a saved version. It does not move a branch.
`git revert` adds a commit that reverses a change. Nothing needs reversing here, since the branch only has to move to a commit that still exists.
`git reflog` only lists where HEAD has been. It does not move the branch.

questions.prompt: History is `one`, `two`, `three`, `four` and `five`. You run `git reset --soft HEAD~2`. How many commits remain on the branch?
hints: reset moves the branch pointer back along the parent links.
HEAD~2 names the commit two steps back from the newest.
Count the commits up to and including that commit.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: reset moves the branch back two commits, so it ends at `three`: 5 − 2 = 3 commits.

questions.onCorrect: The soft mode leaves the removed commits' files staged, ready to be committed again.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count before the reset, and a reset moves the branch back.
That is HEAD~1. The number after the tilde is the number of commits that leave the branch.
HEAD~2 names `three`, and that commit stays on the branch.

questions.prompt: While `git bisect run` is searching, your test script exits with code 125 on one commit because the project does not build there. What does bisect do with that commit?
hints: Ask what the failure to build tells you about this commit.
Most codes mean good or bad, and one special code means neither.

acceptedIdeas: It skips the commit and tests another
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It skips the commit and tests another

questions.onCorrect: The code 125 tells bisect the commit cannot be tested, so it moves on to a neighbouring commit instead.

choices.label: It marks the commit bad
It stops the search with an error
It marks the commit good
It skips the commit and tests another

misconceptions.feedback: A code of 125 is not read as an ordinary failure.
Bisect carries on after a code it cannot use as good or bad.
Only an exit code of 0 means good, and a project that does not build is not good.

questions.prompt: The bug arrived at c6 among c1 to c8. Bisect tests c4 first, and a flaky test fails on it at random, so c4 is reported bad. What happens to the rest of the search?
hints: A bad result tells bisect that the first bad commit is at or before c4.
Ask whether c6 is in the half that is kept.

acceptedIdeas: It searches c1 to c4, so it can never reach c6
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It searches c1 to c4, so it can never reach c6

questions.onCorrect: A test has to give the same answer every time on a given commit, or one wrong answer can send the search into the wrong half.

choices.label: It searches c5 to c8 and still finds c6
It tests c4 again, because the result contradicts itself
It searches c1 to c4, so it can never reach c6
It stops and reports an error

misconceptions.feedback: A bad result means the first bad commit is c4 or earlier, so bisect keeps the lower half. It cannot know the result was a fluke.
Bisect runs each test once and believes the result, so it sees no contradiction to check.
Bisect carries on, and the harm shows in the commit it finally reports.

questions.prompt: A history of 1,500 commits grows to 6,000. How many extra tests, at most, does bisect need for the longer history?
hints: Each doubling of the history adds one halving.
Compare the smallest powers of two that reach each size.
Subtract the smaller number of tests from the larger.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1,500 needs 11 tests, because 2^11 = 2,048 reaches 1,500 and 2^10 = 1,024 does not. 6,000 needs 13, because 2^13 = 8,192 reaches 6,000 and 2^12 = 4,096 does not. The difference is 2.

questions.onCorrect: Growing the history fourfold costs two more tests, because it doubles twice.

misconceptions.feedback: Bisect does not need a test per extra commit, since each test halves the range.
One extra test covers one doubling, and the history here grew by a factor of four.
That is the number of tests for the longer history, not the difference.

questions.prompt: What is the largest number of tests bisect needs for 3,000 commits?
hints: Find the smallest power of two that reaches 3,000.
Powers of two run 2, 4, 8, 16 and so on, doubling each time.
Count how many doublings reach 3,000.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2^11 = 2,048 is too few and 2^12 = 4,096 is enough: 12 tests.

questions.onCorrect: The tests needed are the smallest k such that 2^k is at least the number of commits.

misconceptions.feedback: 2 to the 11th power is 2,048, which falls short of 3,000.
That is how many commits remain after the first test, not the number of tests.

questions.prompt: Bisect is allowed at most 12 tests. What is the largest history, in commits, in which it is sure to find the first bad commit?
hints: Each extra test doubles the number of commits that can be searched.
One test handles 2 commits, two tests handle 4, and so on.
Work out 2 to the 12th power.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each test halves the window, so 12 tests cover 2^12 = 4,096 commits.

questions.onCorrect: Every extra test doubles the history that bisect can handle.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of tests. Each test halves the history, so the number of commits is a power of two.
2^11 is 2,048, which is the limit for 11 tests.
Each test doubles what can be searched, so the limit grows as a power of two and not by 2 per test.

questions.prompt: Your push is rejected with `fetch first`. You run `git fetch` and then `git push` again. What happens?
hints: The host accepts a push only if your branch contains everything the host has.
Ask what `git fetch` changes in your own repository.

acceptedIdeas: It is rejected again, because the fetch did not change your branch
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is rejected again, because the fetch did not change your branch

questions.onCorrect: The fetch brings the commits in, but your branch must still include them, by a merge or a rebase, before the host will accept it.

choices.label: It succeeds, because the fetch brought the host's commits into your branch
It is rejected again, because the fetch did not change your branch
It succeeds, because the fetch told the host which commits you have
It stops with a merge conflict, because the fetch merged the commits

misconceptions.feedback: A fetch updates `origin/main` and stores the commits, but it does not change your own branch.
The host does not need to be told. It checks whether your branch contains its current tip.
A fetch never merges. It changes nothing you are working on.

questions.prompt: Alice has made 2 commits, and Bob has pushed 4 commits from the same starting point. Alice runs `git pull --no-rebase`, which merges Bob's commits into her branch. How many commits does her `main` have that `origin/main` lacks?
hints: After the pull, origin/main still points where the fetch left it.
Count what is on her main and not on origin/main.
Her own commits count, and so does any commit the pull created.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Her 2 own commits and the new merge commit are on her main and not on origin/main: 2 + 1 = 3.

questions.onCorrect: Pushing now would upload those three commits, and the host would accept them as a plain advance.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts her own commits but leaves out the merge commit, which is new and which the host has never seen.
Bob's four commits are on origin/main already, so they are not among the commits that main has and origin/main lacks.
That adds Bob's commits as well, but origin/main already has them.

questions.prompt: A 1,000-line change was shipped as ten pull requests, merged one after another. Pull request 4 has a bug, and pull requests 5 to 10 do not touch its lines. You revert pull request 4. Which pull requests' changes are in `main` afterwards?
hints: A revert undoes one change by adding a new commit.
Ask which pull requests touch the lines that were reverted.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Pull requests 1 to 3 and 5 to 10

questions.onCorrect: Had the change shipped as one pull request, the revert would have undone every line, good or bad.

choices.label: Pull requests 1 to 3 only
Pull requests 1 to 3 and 5 to 10
Pull requests 5 to 10 only
All ten, because a merged pull request cannot be reverted

misconceptions.feedback: A revert adds a commit that reverses one change. It does not roll the branch back, so pull requests 5 to 10 stay.
Pull requests 1 to 3 came before the bug, and the revert does not touch them.
Revert works on any commit in the history, and merged work is exactly what it is used for.

questions.prompt: The version is 1.8.0 and a breaking change is made. What is the new version?
hints: A breaking change raises the leftmost number.
A bump resets every number to its right to zero.
questions.onCorrect: The major number rose by one and the other two went back to zero, so 1.8.0 became 2.0.0.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the patch bump for a bug fix. A breaking change raises the major number.
That is the minor bump for a compatible feature.
The major number does rise, but a bump resets every number to its right to zero.

questions.prompt: `git cat-file -t v1.0` prints `commit`. What kind of tag is `v1.0`?
hints: Think about what the name points at.
A tag with its own message and tagger is an object of its own, with its own type.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A lightweight tag

questions.onCorrect: A lightweight tag is only a pointer, so the type shown is that of the commit it names.

choices.label: An annotated tag
A lightweight tag
A branch
A tag that has not been pushed

misconceptions.feedback: An annotated tag is an object of its own, so `git cat-file -t` prints a different type for it.
The question already calls `v1.0` a tag, so the choice is between the two kinds of tag.
Whether a tag has been pushed is a separate matter. `git cat-file -t` reports only the type of the object the name points at.

questions.prompt: The version is 3.7.2 and you add a backwards-compatible feature. What is the new version?
hints: A compatible feature raises the middle number.
The last number resets to zero.
questions.onCorrect: A minor bump tells users that the release adds something and breaks nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the bump for a bug fix. A new feature raises the minor number.
That is for a breaking change.

questions.prompt: The version is 3.7.2 and you make a breaking change. What is the new version?
hints: A breaking change raises the first number.
The other two return to zero.
questions.onCorrect: A major bump warns users that upgrading may need changes on their side.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the bump for a compatible feature. A breaking change raises the major number.
That is the bump for a bug fix.

flashcards.front: Why can a clone of a Git repository show you the history without contacting the server?
flashcards.back: Every clone contains the complete history, not only the latest files.

flashcards.front: How many parents does the very first commit in a repository have?
flashcards.back: The first commit has no parent, so the answer is 0.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first commit has no parent, so the answer is 0.

flashcards.front: What one word describes version control where every clone holds the full history?
flashcards.back: Distributed: the history is spread across every clone.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Distributed: the history is spread across every clone.

flashcards.front: Which command copies a file's content into the index?
flashcards.back: git add stages the content as it is at that moment, not the file for all time.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: git add stages the content as it is at that moment, not the file for all time.

flashcards.front: Why does a file that was added and then edited show `MM` in `git status --short`?
flashcards.back: The left M compares the index with the last commit and the right M compares the working tree with the index, and both differ.

flashcards.front: What is the working tree's partner place that holds the draft of the next commit called?
flashcards.back: The index, also known as the staging area, holds the draft of the next commit.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The index, also known as the staging area, holds the draft of the next commit.

flashcards.front: A full SHA-1 hash is how many hexadecimal characters long?
flashcards.back: 160 bits at 4 bits per character is 40 characters.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 160 bits at 4 bits per character is 40 characters.

flashcards.front: Which object type holds the contents of one file and no name?
flashcards.back: A blob stores only contents, and the name is held by the tree that lists it.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A blob stores only contents, and the name is held by the tree that lists it.

flashcards.front: Why does changing an old commit change the hash of every later commit?
flashcards.back: Each commit contains its parent's hash, so a changed parent changes the content, and so the hash, of its child.

flashcards.front: Which notation names the parent of the commit you are on?
flashcards.back: HEAD~1 is one step back along the parent links.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: HEAD~1 is one step back along the parent links.

flashcards.front: What does main..feature select?
flashcards.back: The commits reachable from feature that are not reachable from main.

flashcards.front: Which command shows who last changed each line of a file?
flashcards.back: git blame prints each line with the commit that last touched it.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: git blame prints each line with the commit that last touched it.

flashcards.front: What does the file .git/HEAD usually contain?
flashcards.back: It names the current branch, in a line such as ref: refs/heads/main.

flashcards.front: What is a branch, in terms of files?
flashcards.back: A small file naming one commit by its hash, so a branch is a pointer and not a copy.

flashcards.front: How many commits does git switch x create?
flashcards.back: None: it only moves HEAD to x.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: None: it only moves HEAD to x.

flashcards.front: What is the common ancestor from which a three-way merge starts called?
flashcards.back: The merge base is the latest commit that both branches can reach.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The merge base is the latest commit that both branches can reach.

flashcards.front: How many commits does a fast-forward merge create?
flashcards.back: None: it only moves a branch label forward.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: None: it only moves a branch label forward.

flashcards.front: When does Git have to make a merge commit instead of a fast-forward?
flashcards.back: When the branch you merge into has commits of its own, so neither tip is an ancestor of the other.

flashcards.front: Which two letters does `git status --short` print beside a file whose merge conflict is unresolved?
flashcards.back: UU means the file is unmerged on both sides.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: UU means the file is unmerged on both sides.

flashcards.front: Why do edits to lines 2 and 3 of a file conflict even though no line was edited twice?
flashcards.back: Git merges in hunks, and changes that touch or abut count as one place where the histories disagree.

flashcards.front: Which command abandons a merge that stopped on a conflict?
flashcards.back: `git merge --abort` returns the project to its state before the merge.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: git merge --abort returns the project to its state before the merge.

flashcards.front: After rebasing, how many of the replayed commits keep their original hash if the branch started in a different place?
flashcards.back: None: each has a new parent and so a new hash.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: None: each has a new parent and so a new hash.

flashcards.front: Which interactive rebase action folds a commit into the one above it?
flashcards.back: squash combines the commit's changes with the one above and gives one commit.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: squash combines the commit's changes with the one above and gives one commit.

flashcards.front: Why is it risky to rebase commits you have already pushed and others have pulled?
flashcards.back: Rebase replaces them with copies that have new hashes, so the others' histories diverge from yours.

flashcards.front: Which git command makes a new commit that reverses an earlier commit?
flashcards.back: git revert adds a commit that applies the opposite change.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: git revert adds a commit that applies the opposite change.

flashcards.front: What does each of `reset --soft`, `--mixed` and `--hard` do to the index and working tree?
flashcards.back: All move the branch back. Soft leaves both alone, mixed also resets the index, and hard resets the working tree too.

flashcards.front: What is the name of the local record of where HEAD has been?
flashcards.back: The reflog, which lists earlier positions such as `HEAD@{1}`.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The reflog, which lists earlier positions such as HEAD@{1}.

flashcards.front: How many tests, at most, does bisect need for a history of 1,000,000 commits?
flashcards.back: 2^20 is 1,048,576, so twenty halvings are enough.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2^20 is 1,048,576, so twenty halvings are enough.

flashcards.front: Which exit code tells git bisect run that a commit is good?
flashcards.back: Exit code 0, the usual code for success.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Zero, the usual code for success.

flashcards.front: Why does git bisect need a test that gives the same answer every time?
flashcards.back: One wrong answer sends the search into the wrong half, so the commit it reports cannot be trusted.

flashcards.front: Which command downloads commits from the remote without changing your branch?
flashcards.back: git fetch updates origin/main and leaves your branch and files alone.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: git fetch updates origin/main and leaves your branch and files alone.

flashcards.front: Why can origin/main be out of date?
flashcards.back: It is a bookmark that moves only when you fetch, pull or push, so it shows the host as it was at your last contact.

flashcards.front: Which option makes a force-push refuse if someone has pushed since your last fetch?
flashcards.back: `--force-with-lease` only replaces the branch if the host still points where `origin/main` says.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: --force-with-lease only replaces the branch if the host still points where origin/main says.

flashcards.front: Which practice merges small changes to a single main branch at least daily?
flashcards.back: Trunk-based development, with very short branches and feature flags.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Trunk-based development, with very short branches and feature flags.

flashcards.front: Give one reason small pull requests are easier to review and safer to merge.
flashcards.back: Less to read, fewer conflicts, and one change is easy to revert alone.

flashcards.front: What do hosting services call the request to merge a branch, reviewed on a web page?
flashcards.back: A pull request, or in GitLab a merge request.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A pull request, or in GitLab a merge request.

flashcards.front: Which Git object type does an annotated tag create, as reported by `git cat-file -t`?
flashcards.back: An annotated tag is its own object, so the type is tag.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An annotated tag is its own object, so the type is tag.

flashcards.front: What does each number of a semantic version tell a user?
flashcards.back: Major means a breaking change, minor means a compatible feature, and patch means a compatible fix.

flashcards.front: From 2.4.1, which version follows a breaking change?
flashcards.back: A breaking change raises the major number and resets the others to zero, which gives 3.0.0.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A breaking change raises the major number and resets the others to zero.
